‘Diwan-i-Khairat’
, which provided financial assistance to the poor Muslims, orphaned women and widows, and arranged marriages for poor Muslim girls.
Firuz Tughluq was the first Indian ruler to arrange Hajj at state expenditure. He also established a Khairati hospital called
‘Dar-ul-Shafa/Shifa’
where skilled Haqim were employed.
Firuz Shah Tughluq was very fond of the slaves.
There were approximately one lakh eighty thousand slaves working under Firuz Tughluq.
A separate department (
‘Diwan-i-Bandagan’
) was formed for caring of them.
He established a Public Work Department.
It is said that Firuz built
new cities.
Fatehabad
Hisar
Firozpur
Jaunpur, Firozabad etc.

were prominent towns established by him. According to the Firista, Firuz had constructed 40 mosques, 30 schools, 20 palaces, 100 Inns, 200 towns, 100 hospitals, 5 Makabara, 100 public bathrooms, 10 pillars and 150 bridges.
His chiefarchitect was Malik Ghazi Shahana.
The plan and proposal of each building were presented before
‘Diwan-i-Wajarat’
with its expenditure estimate, and only then the required money could be released.
Firuz Tughluq’s reign became famous for constructing the largest network of canals in India.
To facilitate irrigation, he constructed five major canals.
He was the first Sultan of Delhi who imposed irrigation tax named
‘Haqq-i-Sharb’
after seeking the opinion from the Ulemas.
The farmers who used to use the royal canals for irrigation had to give
portion of their produce to the government.
Jizya
was imposed on Brahmins by Firuz Tughluq.
It is noteworthy that by that time Brahmins were kept free from this tax.

Firuz Shah Tughluq planted 1200 new gardens near Delhi due to his interest in horticulture and rehabilitated thirty old orchards of Alauddin period. He also made measures to improve the quality of fruits in his orchards.
Two Pillars (Stambh) of Ashoka were brought to Delhi from
Meerut
and
Topra
(now in Yamuna Nagar district of Haryana) by Firuz Shah Tughluq.
The Topara Pillar (Stambh) was re established near the palace and the mosque of Firozabad.
The Pillar (Stambh) of Meerut was re-installed near the current Bara Hindu Rao Hospital of Delhi.

Sultan Firuz Tughluq of Delhi had commissioned Sanskrit scholars at his court to translate some sanskrit works into persian, often associated with translation of 300 sanskrit manuscripts collected from Jawalamukhi temple into persian.
Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah (1394 - 1412 AD)
was the last ruler of the Tughluq dynasty. During his reign,
Khwaja Jahan
established an independent state of Jaunpur.
Another grandson of Firuz, Nusrat Shah challenged Nasiruddin.
As a result, Tughluq dynasty was divided into two parts, and both claimants ruled the shrunk kingdom of Delhi simultaneously.
Nasiruddin stayed in Delhi and Nusrat Shah in Firozabad. During the reign of Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah,
Timur
, the Great Turk (Turco-Mongol) General of Central Asia, invaded India
This statement was famous with respect to Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah - ‘The sultanate of Shahanshah extends from Delhi to Palam'.
Timur’s invasion (1398 AD) destroyed the Delhi and started the fall of the Tughluq dynasty.
With the death of Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah, the Tughluq dynasty ended in 1412 AD. The warlords of Delhi elected Daulat Khan as Sultan of Delhi in 1413 AD.
But he was defeated by Khizr Khan.
Khizr Khan was the Subedar of Multan, appointed by Timur and later granted him control over Lahore and Dipalpur.
In 1414 AD, he took control of Delhi after the invasion of Timur and laid the foundations of a new lineage Sayyid Dynasty started. He did not assume the title of Sultan.
Lodi Dynasty was established by
Bahlul Khan Lodi
in 1451 AD.
He sat on the throne of Delhi as ‘Bahlul Shah Ghazi’ and got Khutba proclaimed in his name.

His most important victory was over Jaunpur. Bahlul Lodi did not treat Hindus with religious fanaticism. Many reputed Hindu Sardars were in his court; Rai Karan Singh, Rai Pratap Singh, Rai Nar Singh, Rai Trilokchandra and Rai Dadu. He introduced ‘Bahlul coin’ which was the main means of exchange prior to Akbar.
Bahlul Lodi appointed his third son,
Nizam Khan,
as his successor prior to his death, but some of the chiefs opposed him because his mother (Jaiband/Bibi Ambha) was the daughter of a goldsmith.
Some powerful warlords joined Nizam Khan and he sat on the throne as Sultan Sikandarshah on 17 July, 1489 AD. He was the greatest ruler of the Lodi dynasty.
Sikandar Lodi,

in 1504 AD, established a new city called Agra along the Yamuna River to command eastern Rajasthan and routes towards Malwa/Gujarat and made Agra his capital. Sikandar Lodi was a very hard- working, generous but religiously orthodox.
He worked for the improvement and advancement of agriculture and trade.
The measurement scale used for land
‘Gaj-i-Sikandari’
was started at that time. He arranged free meals for the poor.
He prohibited ‘Tazia’ in Muharram and banned Muslim women from visiting ‘Peers’and ‘Mazaars’.
During his reign, a list was made of qualified and skilled persons and was presented every six months before him.
He was an educated and learned person.
He ordered an Ayurvedic treatise to be translated into Persian and named it ‘Farhange Sikandari’.
Lajjat-i-Sikandarshahi’
, a masterpiece of singing, was composed during his reign.
Sikandar Lodi was very fond of hearing Shehnai.
He used to write poems under the nickname
‘Gulrukhi’
Sultan Sikandar abolished the octrai duty on grain.
There was a battle between Maharana Sanga and Ibrahim Lodi at
Khatauli
in 1518 AD.
Ibrahim Lodi was defeated in this battle.
The
first battle of Panipat
took place between Babur and Ibrahim Lodi on
21 April, 1526
A.D.
Ibrahim was defeated and killed on the battle- field.
According to Nayamatullah (Niyamatullah), besides Sultan Ibrahim, no other Sultan of India was killed on the battlefield.
The Vijayanagara Empire was established by
Harihara-I
and
Bukka-I
in
. Their lineage was called Sangama Dynasty as their father’s name was Sangama.
Harihara and Bukka were feudataries of the Kakatiyas of Warangal. After the fall of Warangal at the hands of Delhi Sultans, they shifted to Kampili and become ministers.

When Muhammad Tughluq conquered the Kampili, he imprisoned Harihara and Bukka. It is believed that they accepted Islam religion. They were later sent as Tughluq army commanders towards South. Harihara and Bukka came to Kampili with Tughluq's force and suppressed Kampili revolt. Eventually, they became Hindu again, coming under the influence of a Saint
Vidyaranya
Harihara and Bukka had taken learning from their teacher(Guru)
Vidyaranya
and famous mentor of the Vedas, Sayan, to establish Vijayanagara.
Four dynasties of this empire -
Sangam dynasty
Saluva dynasty
Tuluva dynasty
Aravidu dynasty
The capitals of the Vijayanagara empire were -
Anegundi
Vijayanagara
Penukonda,
and
Chandragiri
and later Vellore.
In 1365, the Vijayanagar army under Kumara Kampana (son of Bukka I) completed the conquest of Pandyan country (Madhurai region) by about 1370.
Kumara Kampana conquered Madurai and merged it into Vijayanagara Empire.
His wife Gangadevi has made a living description of her husband’s victory in her book
‘Madhura Vijayam’
Kumara Kampana
was the son of
Bukka Rai I
After Bukka’s death in 1377 A.D., his son, Harihara II, sat on the throne.
He assumed the title of ‘
Maharajadhiraja

He won the states of Kanara, Mysore, Trichinapalli, Kanchi, etc and rulers such as Ceylon are described as sending ambassadors and annual rich presents. The biggest success of Harihara II was to capture Belgaum and Goa of the Bahamani state in the west.
He was a worshiper of Virupaksha Shiva.
Samant Narasimha Saluva
of Chandragiri removed the last ruler of the Sangama dynasty, Praudha Deva Raya, in 1485 A.D. and took control of the throne and established a new dynasty
‘Saluva Dynasty’
Vira Narasimha

removed the son of Narasimha Saluva (Immadi Narasimha, the last ruler of the Saluva dynasty) from the throne, took control of the throne and laid the foundation of the Tuluva dynasty. His younger brother
Krishnadeva Raya
(1509-1529 AD) sat on the throne after the death of Veer Narasimha.
Krishnadeva Raya, the ruler of Vijayanagara, fought the
battle of Golconda
with Sultan Quli Qutb Shah of Golconda.
The army of Qutb Shahi was defeated.
The reign of Krishnadeva Raya is considered to be a classical era of Telugu literature in Vijayanagara.
Eight Telugu poets of his court were regarded as eight pillars of his literary assembly and known as
Ashtadiggajas
Therefore, his reign was also called the golden age of Telugu literature.
Krishnadeva Raya had assumed the title of
‘Andhra Bhoj’
Krishnadeva Raya himselfwas a poet and writer of outstanding ability.
His main composition-
‘Amuktamalyada’
, is one of the five epics of Telugu language.
He established
Nagalapuram
town.
He also constructed temples like
‘Hazara Rama’
and
‘Vitthala (Shree Vijaya Vitthala)’
During his time, the Portuguese traveller
'Domingo Paes’
travelled to the Vijayanagara empire.
Babur, in his autobiography, described Krishnadeva Raya as the most powerful ruler of India.
Persian ambassador
Abdur Razzaq
came to Vijayanagara during the reign of
Devaraya II
, the most august ruler of the Sangama dynasty.
The translation of Mahabharata in Telugu was started by
Nannaya
in the 11th century, which was completed by
Tikkana
in the 13th century and again by the
Yerranna
in the 14th century.
These three are famous as the '
Kavitrayi
' of Telugu literature.
In the famous
Battle of Talikota
, the combined forces offour Deccan sultanates (Bijapur, Bidar, Ahmadnagar, Golconda) defeated Vijayanagara in
January 1565 AD
Barar
was not included in that combined Forces. According to the Firista, this battle was fought in Talikota, but the actual area of war was situated between two villages named Rakshasi and Tangadi.
During the Battle of Talikota, the ruler of Vijayanagara was
Sadashiva Raya
but the real power was in the hands of his minister
Rama Raya
Hussain Nizamashah killed Rama Raya in this battle.
Tirumal
after dethroning Sadashiva in Penukonda, sat on the throne and laid the foundation of the
Aravidu Dynasty (1570-1672 AD)
His successor was
Shri Rang-I
Venkata II
became the ruler after Rang I.
He made Chandragiri his headquarters.
It was the last dynasty in the series of great rulers of Vijayanagara.
Venkata II a was contemporary of King Wodeyar, who established the kingdom of Mysore in 1612.

The main source of revenue in Vijayanagara empire was the taxes on the land/farm. The land was well-surveyed. Normally, the land tax was one-third to one-sixth of the yield. It depends upon land category and crop quality. The tax named
‘Shist’
(Rai-rekha) was the main source of state income.
Central Department of Revenue was called
‘Athavane’
(Asthvan or Athvan).
The present name of the
Dwarasamudra
, the capital of the Hoysala Dynasty, is
Halebidu,
which is in Hassan district of Karnataka.
Its reputation is because of its heritage architecture.
Among the Halebidu temples, the ancient temple of Hoysaleshwara is very famous.
This temple belongs to 12th - 13th century.
During the reign of Hoysala ruler
Narasimha I
, the architect Kedroz constructed the temple under the supervision of Chief Officer of the Public Works Department,
Ketamal
Chennakeshava temple, built in Hoysala period, is located in Belur. This temple was built by Vishnuvardhana, the ruler of the Hoysala dynasty.
The ruins of Hampi (located in the present Central Karnataka) represent the ancient capital of the Vijayanagara Empire.
The
Virupaksha Temple
was built in the Vijayanagara period in 7th century CE and is located right here.
Hampi
is also included in the list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
The
Vitthal Temple
(Hampi) was built by Krishnadeva Raya (1509 - 1529 A.D.), and continued under Achyuntaraya, one of the great rulers of the Tuluva dynasty of the Vijayanagara Empire.
Sultans of the
Slave Dynasty
ruled from 1206 to 1290 AD.
Khalji Dynasty
ruled from 1290 to 1320 AD.
The rulers of the
Tughluq Dynasty
ruled from 1320 to 1414 AD. Sayyid Dynasty ruled from 1414 to 1451 AD.
The rulers of
Lodi Dynasty ruled
from 1451 to 1526 AD. During Sultanate period, rule of Tughluq dynasty was the longest.
Most of the Sultans and Amirs were Turks.

Sultan was the head of central government. Similarly, during the Sultanate Period, those often employed in all the influential positions were called the Amir. These Amirs had a great effect when the Sultan was ineligible and weak or under-age.
Administrative departments and the rulers who started these departments are as follows –
Diwan-i-Mustakhraj
(Department of Revenue) - Alauddin Khalji
Diwan-i-Riyasat
(Department of Market Control) - Alauddin Khalji
Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi
(Agriculture Department) - Muhammad- Bin Tughluq
Diwan-i-Khairat
(Charity Department) - Firuz Tughluq
Diwan-i-Bandagan
- Firuz Tughluq
Diwan-i-Arz
was related to Army Department
Diwan-i-Risalat
was related to religious issues and to overseeing foreign affairs.
Diwan-i-Insha
was related to Government Correspondence
Diwan-i-Wizarat
was related to financial matters/revenue department.

Wizarat was an institution recognized by the Islamic administration. During the reign of Mahmud Ghazni (in Ghaznavid administration), Abbas Fazal - Bin-Ahmad, who was skilled in governing the administration, became the first wazir.
The prime minister of the state was called
Wazir
Wazir was mainly the chief of revenue department
(Diwan-i-Wizarat)
. From this point of view, he used to take care of Lagaan, tax system, donations and, military expenditures etc.
Tughluq period was the golden period of Indian Muslim Wizarat. At the time of Firuz Tughluq, the post of the Wazir reached its peak position.
Army organization and the division of posts were done on the basis of the decimal system.
The head of the troop of the horsemen was called
‘Sarkhel’
There was a
‘Sipahsalar’
above ten Sarkhels, one
‘Amir’
above ten Sipahsalars, one
‘Malik’
above ten Amirs and one
‘Khan’
over ten Maliks.
Sultan was the Chief Commander of the army.
Firuz Tughluq levied taxes, keeping the laws of the Islam in mind.
He permitted four taxes approved in the Quran -
Kharaj
Jizya
Khums
and
Zakat
. Khums was the one-fifth share of looted money.
In the war, the enemies of the state were looted by his people.
4/5 part
of this loot was distributed among the soldiers, and the remaining

was deposited in the treasury, but Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad Tughluq kept 4/5 in the treasury, and the remaining 1/5 was divided among the soldiers. In the Sultanate period, the smallest unit of governance was village and, main village functionaries were Khut, Muqaddam and Patwari, working in close coordination with muqti for revenue collection.
Chaudhary
was the highest official of land revenue at the village level.
The Sultanate period had two major currencies -
Jital
and
Tanka
Iltutmish was the first Turk ruler, who introduced Arabic coins.
He introduced the two main coins namely Tanka of silver, and Jital of copper.
The ratio of Tanka and Jital was
The name of the last Khalifa of Baghdad was first mentioned on the coin of Alauddin Masood Shah (1242 - 46 AD).
The last Khalifa of Baghdad was Khalifa-al-Mustasim (1242 - 58 AD ). The name of
Khalifa-al-Mustansir
was mentioned on coins of Iltutmish. Hadees was an Islamic law, while the Zawabit was related to state law.
Qutbuddin Aybak built
‘Adhai Din Ka Jhopara’
mosque in Ajmer and
‘Quwwat-ul-Islam’
mosque near Raipithora Fort in Delhi. Construction of
Qutub Minar
was started in Delhi by Aybak, which was completed by Iltutmish.
Iltutmish built Sultangarhi, Hauz-e-Shamsi, Shamsi Eidgaah, Jama Masjid Shamsi (Badayun). Atarkin-ka-Darwaza (Nagaur) etc. Alauddin Khalji built
Alai Darwaza
near the Qutub Minar. It was built with red sandstones and white marble, and it was completed in 1311 AD.
Alauddin Khalji built Hazar Sutun and Hauz-e-Alai in the Delhi (Siri fort). Ukha Mosque (Bayana Rajasthan) was built by Malik Kafur Sultani during reign of Sultan Mubarakshah Khalji.
The tomb of Sultan Balban, located in Mehrauli, New Delhi, built by himself, was the first tomb built in a purely Indo-Islamic style in India.
Ghiyasuddin Tughluq
(1320 - 25 AD), after the foundation of the Tughluq dynasty, established a city in Delhi and named it
‘Tughluqabad’
The Moth Masjid was built during the reign of Sikandar Lodi.

Sikandar Lodi’s tomb was built by Sultan Ibrahim Lodi. Kirti Stambha was built by Rana Kumbha after his victory over Malwa. It was built under the supervision of Jaita while Atri and Mahesh were its panegyrists.
Abul Hassan Yaminuddin Khusrau, often called Amir Khusrau, was born in 1253 AD at Patiyali in present-day Kasganj district in Uttar Pradesh. Khusrau was called
‘Tuti- i - Hind’
Some of his famous compositions were
Miftah-ul-Futuh
Khazain ul-Futuh
(Tarikh-i-Alai),
Ashika
Nuh Sipihr
and
Tughluq namah
. He referred to himself as a 'Turkish-Indian'.
Amir Khusrau himself said that he knew, Sanskrit and other Indian languages, which are a part of Hindavi.
In India, Amir Khusrau was the originator of the early form of the musical genre known as
Qawwali
New Persian poetry style, ‘Sabk - i - Hindi’ or Hindustani style, was started by Amir Khusrau.
Musical instruments
‘Tabla’
and
‘Sitar’
were made prevalent in the 13th/14th century by Amir Khusrau.
The development of Persian literature in India started with the advent of Muslims.
After the establishment of Delhi Sultanate, the Persian language was granted the status of official language.
Tabakat-i-Nasiri
is a treatise of
Minhaj-us-Siraj
(Minhaj i-Siraj) dedicated to Sultan Nasiruddin Mahmud.
Ziauddin Barani composed the ‘
Tarik -i-Firozshahi
’and ‘
Taj-ul-Masir
’ was written by Sadruddin Muhammad Hassan Nizami.
Yahiya Bin Ahmad Sarhindi wrote ‘
Tarikh-i-Mubarakshahi
’, which is the principal source regarding the history of Sayyid rulers under the patronage of Sayyid Mubarakshah.
Rana Kumbha was a patron of music, literature and art. He wrote texts on music,
Sangeet Raja
(also known as Sangita Mimansa).
The Tughluq dynasty ruler Firuz Shah Tughluq wrote his memoir as
Futuhat-i-Firuz Shahi
The Polo game in India was introduced by Turks.
It is known that Qutbuddin Aybak was fond of Polo (Chaugan). He died in 1210 AD while playing this game.
During the Sultanate period, people of high religious and judicial positions (Ulema), were called ‘Dastar Bandan’because they used to wear official Turban on their heads.
Jauhar was committed by Rajput women to protect their honour from Muslim invaders.

chapters.title: Provincial Dynasty of North India and Deccan Province

runs: Jaunpur was founded by
Firuz Shah Tughluq
in memory of his cousin
Jauna Khan
(Muhammad-Bin Tughluq).
Jaunpur became an independent state during the reign of Sultan Mahmud Shah II (1394.).
It was established by Malik Sarwar, who founded the independent Sharqi Kingdom.
Malik Sarwar
was a slave of Muhammad Shah II.
Sultan gave him the title of Malik-Us Sharq (the Lord of the East) and Khwaja-i-Jahan.
Sharqi rulers continued Jaunpur’s independence for nearly 85 years but in
Bahlul Lodi
defeated its last ruler
Hussain Shah Sharqi
and made Jaunpur a part of Delhi Sultanate again.
Ibrahim Shah Sharqi
(1402 - 1440 AD) (as per Gazetteer of Jaunpur) was the greatest ruler of the Sharqi Dynasty of Jaunpur.
During his reign, a new type of style emerged, which was called ‘
Sharqi style
During this time, the cultural fame of Jaunpur spread all around and the state became famous as the
‘Siraz-i-Hind’(Siraz of India)
Vidyapati
has beautifully described Jaunpur and Ibrahim Shah in ‘
Kirtilata Kavya
Ali Shah’s brother Shahi Khan sat on the throne of Kashmir as Zain-ul-Abidin in 1420 A.D. He became the greatest ruler of Kashmir.
He abolished ‘Jizya’ and banned cow slaughter. He got "Mahabharata" & "Rajtarangini" translated in Persian language.
‘Zaina Lank’ island was built by
Zain-ul-Abidin
in ‘Wular Lake’. Zain-ul-Abidin (1420-70 AD) is called ‘
Akbar of Kashmir
’ due to religious tolerance and good deeds.
Zafar Khan
declared himself Sultan of Gujarat in 1407 AD, adopting the name ‘Sultan Muzaffar Shah’.
He defeated the ruler of Malwa, Hoshang Shah and occupied Dhar, but later he returned his kingdom.
Later, Fateh Khan sat on the throne in 1458 AD.
He took the title of ‘Abul Fateh Mahmood’, but in history he became famous as Mahmud Begada.
His main victories were the forts of Champaner and Girnar.
Bahmani Kingdom
was founded during the Muhammad-bin Tughluq’s reign as a result of the rebellion of Amiran-e-Sadah in Deccan.
Zafar Khan
(Hasan Gangu, 1347 - 1358 AD) a Sardar in 1347 AD, assuming the title of Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah, sat on the throne and laid the foundation of the Bahmani kingdom.
He made Gulbarga the capital of his newly established kingdom and named it Hasanabad.
To govern his empire, he divided it into four provinces of Gulbarga, Daulatabad, Berar and Bidar.
Ibrahim Adilshah II
, the ruler of Bijapur, was a skillful administrator, poet and a generous patron of arts.
His people used to address him with the title of
‘Jagatguru’
due to his generous and broad (tolerant) approach. He was also called ‘Ablababa’or ‘Friend of the poor’because of his nature of helping the poor.
Ibrahim Adil Shah II composed music collection
‘Kitab-i-Nauras’
In the same era, Firishta had completed the work of a famous historic book named
‘Tarikh-i-Firishta’
Ibrahim established a new capital, Naurasapur city.
The mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah of Bijapur is known as
‘Gol Gumbaz’
. It is one of the largest historic buildings in India and one of the world’s largest domes.
Gujari Mahal
was built by King Man Singh Tomar between 1486-1516 A.D. century. Currently, Gujari Mahal is converted into Museum.
Successor states of Bahamani
Shah

Devotional Worship had a long history of almost a thousand years across the subcontinent. The early medieval Bhakti movement originated in Dravida region and began to spread to the north during the late medieval ages (13th-14th centuries onwards) when north India was under Islamic rule.
Some of the earliest Bhakti movements (6th Century) were led by Vaishnava Alvars and Nayanars of South (Shaiva). Bhakti Movement spread with the rise of the great philosopher
Adi Shankaracharya
in South India in 8th century who propagated pure monism
‘Advaitavada’
Bhakti Movement was reborn in the 15th-16th century A.D. when the
Kabir, Nanak, Tulsi, Sur, Meerabai
etc. encouraged the movement.
In medieval India, the emergence of Sufis helped in promoting harmony in society.
They used to do meditation and practised spiritual disciplines such as remembrance and devotional practices like 'Sama' and sometimes breath-focused remembrance.

Sufism originated within Islam and later some strands developed theosophical systems adopting tradition such as Neoplatonism and other currents. Some believe that four philosophies influenced the Sufism –
(1) Advaitavada and Vishishta Dvaitavada of Aryans
(2) New Aflatuni theory
(3) Liberal thinking
(4) Deep rooted knowledge of Islam
They took the help of holy songs and music to spread unity and harmony in society and to arouse a state of spiritual ecstasy in their audience.
Kamarupa

was an ancient Indian state situated roughly in Assam. Vaishnavism in Kamarupa was popularized by Shankaradeva, the founder of Ekasarana sect. They stressed devotion to one deity–krishna (identified with Vishnu). They also opposed both rituals and idolatry. They were known as
Chaitanya
of Assam.
Shuddha Advaitavada
is the “purely non-dual” philosophy propounded by Shri Vallabhacharya, the founder and guru of the Vallabha sect.
Vallabhacharya
was the son of Telugu Brahmin Shri Lakshmana Bhatta of Somyazi clan, who is said to have developed the views of
Vishnu Swami
into Shuddha Advaita or pure non-dualism.
The founder of
‘Dvaitavada’
was
Madhvacharya
Nimbarkacharya
was the founder of
‘Dvaitadvaitavada (Dvait-Advait Vad)’
and
Ramanujacharya
was the founder of
‘Vishishtadvaitavad’
. Nimbarkacharya is related to the
‘Sanaka’
sect.
Ramananda was the promoter of the Bhakti Movement in northern India. He was born in the Kanyakubja Brahmin family of Prayaga (Prayagraj) in 1299 AD.
These used to believe in
‘Saguna’
God.
He was the first Bhakti saint who promoted his messages in the Hindi language.
was one of the 12 disciples of Ramananda. He was born near Varanasi to a widowed Brahmin and grew up with a weaver couple Neeru and Neema.
‘Bijak’
is a compilation of the works of Saint Kabir. It is a holy book of those who believe in the Kabirpanthi sect.
'Sabad
'Sakhi'
and
'Ramaini'
are compositions of Kabir but his dialogues with Dharmadasa are found in the book ‘
Amarmul/Anurag Sagar
Saint Malukdasa
was born in the family of Lala Sundar Das Khatri in 1574 AD in Kada (present-day Kaushambi district of Uttar Pradesh).
Guru Ghasidas
was born on 18 December 1756 AD in Giraudpuri village in Balodabazar-Bhatapara district of Chhattisgarh.
12 Jyotirlingas
devoted to lord Shiva are found in different parts of India.
These are - Kedarnath, Vishwanath, Vaidyanath, Mahakaleshwara, Omkareshwara, Nageshwara, Somnath, Trayambakeshwara, Grishneshwara, Bhimashankara, Mallikarjun Swami and Rameshwaram.
Guru Nanak
was born in
Talwandi in Punjab
in 1469 AD. Now this place is called
‘Nankana Sahib’
It is located in Nankana Sahib district of western Punjab (now in Pakistan).
Guru Nanak died in
at
Kartarpur
(present day in Pakistan).
Guru Nanak
(1469 - 1539 AD) was the founder of Sikh religion during the reign of Sikandar Lodi (1489 - 1517 AD).
Nanak believed in
monotheism
and emphasized the worship of the one formless God (IK Onkar).
Guru Nanak says, "God doesnot ask about social class or birth; you must find your true home."
Guru Nanak started the community kitchen known as
‘Guru Ka Langar’
. The followers used to eat together without paying any attention to the caste.
Mirabai
was the only daughter of Ratan Singh Rathore of Merta.
She was born in village Kudaki of Merta in 1498 AD. She was married to Prince Bhojraja, the eldest son of famous ruler Rana Sanga of Mewar.
Namdev

"Emperor without Empire"
Ibrahim Zauq and Asad Ullah Khan Ghalib taught poetry to Bahadur Shah Zafar. Hasan Askari was sufi saint and Pir to Zafar.

Bahadur Shah Zafar got Rs 1 lakh per month from the East India Company as pension, which consisted of Rs. 99000 given in Delhi and one thousand rupees for regular family expenses in Lucknow. He died in 1862 A.D.
Chin Qilich Khan
aka
Nizam-ul-Mulk
founded the independent Kingdom of Hyderabad in 1724. Nizam became the real king after the death of the Mughal governor
Mubariz Khan
in the
battle of Sakhar - Kheda
of Deccan,
Sawai Jai Singh (Jai Singh II)
(1688 - 1743 A.D.) of Amber was a Rajput king of the 18th century.
He established
‘Jaipur’
city and made it the centre of science and art.
He built well equipped observatories in Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura and Varanasi. He patronised the translation of‘‘Euclid's Geometry” in Sanskrit.
He organized two Ashvamedh sacrifices during his reign.

According to one theory, Vasco da Gama reached India with the help of an Arab navigator Ahmad Ibn Majid, but according to historical & authentic evidence, the person who helped Vasco da Gama reach Indian port of Calicut was a Gujarati sailor. Vasco da Gama sailed to the Western Coast of India, at the port of Calicut on May 20, 1498. He had successfully discovered a new and alternative sea route to India from Europe. Zamorin (Zamorin was the ancestral title of the rulers of Calicut), then the ruler of Calicut, welcomed Vasco da Gama. The arrival of Vasco da Gama in India started a new era of trade between Portuguese and Indians. Vasco da Gama returned with the cargo having 60 times more profit than the expedition cost, in the business of Black Pepper which was enough to lure other merchants to India.
Francisco de Almeida
arrived in India as first
Portuguese Viceroy
. In the light of Portuguese trade interests and to establish Portuguese authority in the Indian Ocean, Almeida rendered the
Blue Water Policy
Afonso de Albuquerque

came as the Governor of the Portuguese region in India 1509 A.D. after Almeida. In 1510 A.D., he snatched Goa from Adil-Shahi Sultanate, the rulers of Bijapur, and established his authority there. He is known as the real founder of the Portuguese power in India.
Albuquerque in 1511 A.D. captured
Malacca,
an important South-East Asian Market and, in 1515, captured
Hormuz
situated at the mouth of Persian Gulf.
Nuno da Cunha
assumed the Governor office after Lopo Vaz de Sampaio in 1529 A.D. and remained the Governor until the end of 1538 A.D.
A new sea route to India was discovered by Portuguese traveller
Vasco da Gama
whereas Columbus, a traveller originally from Italy and financed by Spain discovered America, and
Tasman
of Holland discovered
Van Diemen's Land
(currently Tasmania) and
New Zealand

. The first European to reach Australia was English Navigator Willem Janszoon (1712-1780), while the British Navigator Captain Cook arrived at Australia in 1770 A.D. (about 164 years later, when Willem Janszoon reached to Australia). Captain Cook is credited with surveying Australia’s east coast and laying foundation of British rule there.

In 1503, at Cochin, first Portuguese Fort (first European Fort in India) was constructed by Afonso de Albuquerque (during his first visit to India in 1503 A.D.). The fort was named as ‘Emmanuel Fort’.
The sequence of Arrival of European Companies to India is:
Portuguese
Dutch
English
Danish
and
French
Portuguese were the first to arrive in
and were last to leave India in
(de Jure transfer took place in August 1962).
In 1961 the Portuguese Governor-General of Goa was
Manuel Antonio Vassalo e Silva
Jose Ferreira Bossa
was the Governor- General of Goa when India gained Independence in 1947.
Among all European powers, Portuguese were the first to establish Sea trading centers in India.
Portuguese in 1500 A.D. established their first factory at Calicut.

In 1535 A.D. Ghiyasuddin Mahmud Shah, the ruler of Bengal, promised the Portuguese to establish the forts in Chittagong and Satgaon, in return for their assistance of the ruler during the Sher Shah Suri’s invasion of Bengal.
Hooghly was used as a base by Portuguese for plundering activities in the Bay of Bengal.
In 1632 A.D., Mughal king Shahjahan, ordered Bengal Subedar Qasim Khan to destroy the establishments of Portuguese in Hooghly and imprison thousands of Portuguese residents.
Job Charnock,
head of the factory of Qasim Bazar, selected Sutanuti instead at Hooghly for English Trading Center. This is how he established Calcutta as a Base of Englishmen.

In 1602 A.D., Dutch (Holland) States General Chartered the establishment of a United East India Company. It had a Capital of6,500,000 Guilders. This company had a monopoly to do trade and to attack and win territories in India and eastern countries. Its eastern centre was situated in
Batavia

(currently Jakarta). Eastern Empire of Dutch was operated and administered by this company. Its partners worked as a private group. Dutch constructed William Fort at Modern Kochi in 1663 A.D. after defeating Portuguese. Kochi in 1814 AD was included in British settlements under the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1814.
In 1600 A.D., a trading company
English East India Company
or '
The Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies' was founded in England
Akbar
was the King of India during establishment.

The Levant Company (1592) was granted a monopoly to trade with Ottoman Empire (The Levant) and its eastern areas (including India). They traded in Silk, spices etc. After the ‘Royal Charter’ of Queen Elizabeth I, the East India company was provided with exclusive 15-year monopoly on English trade with all countries east of Cape of Good Hope, which included India.
During the Reign of Jahangir, in
A.D., East India Company established its first temporary factory at
Masulipatnam
. In
A.D., English established their first permanent factory at
Surat
Dutch established their factory at Surat in
A.D. followed by French in
A.D.
Thomas Best was the English officer who defeated Portuguese at a place named
Swally
In 1662 A.D., King of Britain Charles II married Portuguese Princess Catherine and received Mumbai as a gift which was leased to East India Company on payment of
10 Pound annually
(under the Marriage Treaty of 1961).
A British official
John Child,

in 1688 A.D., surrounded Mughal ports in Bombay and other Mughal ports on the western coast and tried to imprison Hajj travellers going to Mecca as a result of which Aurangzeb expelled him from India.
First Carnatic War (1746-48 A.D.)
was just an extension of the War of Succession in Austria which started in 1740.

In 1746 English and French started war without the consent of their home nations in India. English Navy under the leadership of Commodore Bernett seized French Ships, this was the immediate reason for war. During the first Carnatic War, the Nawab of Carnatic,
Anwaruddin,
sent an Army of 10,000 men under the leadership of
Mahfooz Khan
to attack French. Under the leadership of Captain Paradise, the French defeated the Force of Nawab at a place called
St. Thome
on the bank of Adyar River. With the end of the war in Europe, the war in India also ended with the
Treaty of Aix - la - Chapelle (1748 A.D.).
Austrian Succession war ended and Madras was again granted to English.
Dupleix

for the first time used tactics that guided the future campaigns of English men. It was Dupleix who appointed European forces into Indian Courts on Indian expense and interfered in the internal conflicts of kingdoms in the light of European interests and sown the seeds of European rule in India.
Colbert
, a minister of
Louis XIV
, founded
French East India Company
in 1664 A.D. which is also known as
Compagnie Francaise Pour le Commerce des Indes Orientales

(or Compagnie francaise des Indes orientales) in 1667 A.D. Francois Caron headed an expedition to India setting up a factory in Surat in 1668 A.D. Marcara, a Persian who accompanied Caron founded another French factory in Masulipatnam in 1669 A.D. after obtaining permission from the Sultan of Golconda.
Dutch established their first factory at
Masulipatnam
. In Bengal, they established their first factory at
Pipali
. In 1676 A.D. Dutch left the factory at Pipali and established new factory at Balasore. The trade with Bengal started properly when Dutch in 1653 A.D. established their establishment in
Chinsurah
. In Chinsurah, the Dutch fort was called Gustavus Fort.
Europeans obtained high-grade opium and Saltpetre from Bihar. Bihar was famous for opium production during British rule.
The chronology of arrivals of European powers in India is as follows – Portuguese, Dutch, English, Danes and French respectively.

chapters.title: East India Company and Nawabs of Bengal

runs: Murshid Quli Khan was the last Governor of Bengal who was independently appointed by Mughal King.
Murshid Quli Khan shifted his Capital to
Maksudabad
from Dhaka and named it
Murshidabad
. He started Izara System in the land settlement.
Alivardi Khan
(1740-1756 A.D.) comparing Europeans with the Honeybees, said that ifthey are left undisturbed, they will give you honey, and if try to disturb them they will bite you till death.
After the death of Alivardi Khan, his grandson
Siraj-ud-Daula
succeeded to the throne of Bengal.
The Black Hole tragedy

took place during his reign on 20th June 1756 A.D. According to one of the 23 survivors, J.Z. Holwell, 146 English prisoners were put in a cell with a dimension of18 feet in length and 14 feet 10 inches in breadth. 123 of them died due to suffocation and only 23 survived. This incident is known as
Black Hole tragedy
. Contemporary Muslim historian
Ghulam Hussain
in his book ‘Siyar-ul Mutakherin’ has not mentioned this incident.

Robert Clive is known as the founder of the English Empire in India who defeated the forces of Bengal’s Nawab Siraj-ud-Daula in the Battle of Plassey (presently known as Palasi) on 23rd June, 1757 A.D. and sown the seeds of British rule in India. The Battlefield of Plassey is situated on the Banks of Bhagirathi River in Nadia district of West Bengal. Robert Clive was the Governor in 1758- 60 A.D. and
in India. During this period he signed
Allahabad Treaty
with Nawab of Awadh Shuja-ud-Daula and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II During his governorship
White Mutiny
broke out among English soldiers.
Plundering of resources of Bengal by the British Company was started during Clive’s governorship.

Mir Qasim (1760-63 A.D.) was the ablest among the successors of Alivardi Khan. As a ‘Faujdar’ of Poornia and Rangpur, Mir Qasim had already proven his ability. To save his courtiers from repeated conspiracies by Britishers and to avoid interference from Englishmen, Mir Qasim shifted his Capital to Munger from Murshidabad so as to stay away from Calcutta. He consolidated his army using European methods. He made arrangements in Munger for the manufacturing of
Matchlock guns
. Mir Qasim also took some brave steps so as to improve the economic conditions in Bengal. The officers involved in embezzlement were fined heavily, some new taxes were introduced
The Combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula (Nawab of Awadh), and Mughal King Shah Alam II were defeated by Britishers in the Battle of Buxar on
22/23 October, 1764 AD
. English army was led by
Hector Munro
Henry Vansittart

was the then Governor of Bengal. This victory of Britishers made the English a great power in northern India and contenders for supremacy over the whole country. The area up to Allahabad was now under the British and the door of Delhi was now open for British. Battle of Buxar changed the course of Indian History. During this battle,
Mir Jafar
was Nawab of Bengal and Delhi was ruled by
Shah Alam II
. By the treaties of Allahabad (August, 1765) Shah Alam II agreed to reside at Allahabad, under the company’s protection. Nawab Shuja-ud-Daula surrendered Allahabad and Kora to Emperor Shah Alam II.
Shah Alam II issued a decree granting
Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa
to the East India Company.
Robert Clive
became the governor of Bengal and started
Dual government
system in Bengal.
The Company appointed two deputy Diwans,
Mohammad Raza Khan
for Bengal and
Raja Shitab Roy

for Bihar to exercise Diwani functions. Rohilla Sardar Ghulam Qadir annexed Delhi in July 1788, and August 1788, he ousted Shah Alam II and made him blind. During the time of Shah Alam II in 1803, Delhi fell completely to East India Company. Shah Alam II and his two successors Akbar II (1806-37 AD) and Bahadur Shah II (1837-57 AD) were mere pensioners of the East India Company.
The British came to Sylhet (then Sylhet was part of Bengal Presidency) in 1765 AD after acquiring the Diwani right of Bengal. After the War of Burma,
David Scott

tried to connect Assam (Brahmaputra Valley) with Sylhet through roads to Jaintia and Garo Hill areas, but faced a very tough resistance from the Khasi tribes who lived in these areas under the leadership of
Tirot Sing
K.M. Panikar
said that from 1757 to 1773 AD the Company made Bengal a ‘State of Robbers’.
Ranjit Singh
was born to the chief of Sukerchakia Misl on 13th November, 1780 A.D.
Treaty of Amritsar
was signed between Maharaja Ranjit Singh and British East India Company on 25th April, 1809 A.D. Ranjit Singh captured
Multan
Kashmir
in 1819 and Peshawar and North-West frontier (Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa) in 1834 A.D..
In 1798 AD,
Zaman Shah

attacked Punjab. While returning, his cannons accidentally fell into the Jhelam River (some sources refer for Chenab River but Jhelam River is authenticated by many historians). These cannons were sent back to Jaman Shah by Ranjit Singh. Happy with this gesture of Ranjit Singh, Jaman Shah allowed Ranjit Singh to rule Lahore. As a result, in 1799 A.D., Ranjit Singh took control of
Lahore

and made it his Capital. Zaman Shah gave him the title of Raja (in return of his service and providing tanks and artileries) and appointed him as the Subedar of Lahore. He also captured Amritsar from Bhangi Misl in 1802. Now, both the political capital
‘Lahore’
and religious capital
‘Amritsar’
were under the control of Ranjit Singh.
Ranjit Singh was an able ruler. He once said, “God wants me to see all the religions as one, so he took the light of my other eye”.
Shahshuja, descendant of Ahmed Shah Abdali gifted
Kohinoor diamond
to Ranjit Singh.
His son
Kharak Singh
succeeded Ranjit Singh after the laters death in 1839. He was an
opium

addict. During his reign two opposite groups, one consisting of Dogra Brothers - Dhyan Singh, Ghulab Singh and Suchet Singh other included Sandhawaliya Sardar (an aid of Chait Singh) Atar Singh, Lahna Singh and his nephew Ajeet Singh, and Dogras (Dhyan Singh, Gulab Singh and Suchet Singh) were the main reason of growing chaos in Punjab.
Battle of Chillianwala was fought on 13th January 1849 A.D. between English forces led by
Lord Gough
and Sikh forces led by
Sher Singh
. The war ended undecided.
Lord Dalhousie
was the Governor-General of India during this war.
Maharaja Duleep Singh

was the last ruler of Sikh Empire. He ruled from 1843 to 1849 AD. He converted to Christianity and travelled to Russia. Later in 1886 A.D. he again accepted Sikhism. He died in Paris in 1893 AD. His funeral took place in England. In 1849 AD, after the Anglo-Sikh war, Punjab was annexed by Britishers and Duleep Singh was sent to Britain on a pension in 1854 A.D. After the annexation of Punjab, in 1849 A.D. Lord Dalhousie made a three-member body consisting of
Sir Henry Lawrence
as Board’s President and,
John Lawrence
and
Charles Grenville Mansel
as members to administer Punjab.
The
First Anglo-Mysore war
in 1767-69 A.D. made Haidar Ali victorious. The war ended in April, 1769 AD with the
Treaty of Madras
. During this the Governor of Bengal was Harry Verelst (1734-85).
The
Second Anglo Mysore War

(1780-84 AD) - During this war, Haidar Ali made an alliance with Nizam and Marathas against Britishers. In July 1780 A.D. Haidar attacked Carnatic and on 10 September 1780 AD, colonel Baillie was defeated by the combined forces of Haidar Ali and Tipu in the battle of Pollilur (other name Perambakam). In 1781 A.D. Haidar Ali faced
Sir Eyre Coote
who defeated Haidar Ali at Porto Novo (July, 1781 A.D.), Pollilur (In this war, Haider Ali was out rightly defeated but his army faced heavy loss during this) and Sholingur.
Tipu Sultan made
Srirangapattnam
his Capital where he established
Jacobin Club
and became its member. He planted the tree of liberty in his capital as a sign of friendship between Mysore and France.

Tipu sent ambassadors to contemporary foreign states and also established their embassies to maintain friendly relations and to gather help from them against the Britishers. These foreign states included - Iran, Istanbul, Afghanistan, France.
The
Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790-92
A.D.
ended with the
Treaty of Srirangapattna (March 1792
A.D.

. The treaty fo Seringapatam (Srirangapatna) was signed in March 1792 A.D. between Tipu Sultan of Mysore and Lord Cornwallis on behalf of British East India Company. The agreement also included representatives of the Nizam of Hyderabad and Maratha Empire, requiring Tipu to cede halfofhis Kingdom. Tipu Sultan died fighting in the
Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799
A.D.

. All the members of his family were imprisoned in Vellore. British Commanders like Arthur Wellesley (brother of Governor General of Bengal Lord Wellesley), Stuart and General Harris led this war from the English side. In the happiness of this victory, the Lord Society of Ireland conferred the title of
Marquess

to Wellesley. After the war, a minor Krishnaraja Wodeyar III (Mummadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar) from Wodeyar dynasty was placed on the Mysore throne and the British took possession of Kanara, Coimbatore, and Srirangapattnam.
Begum Samru

(1750-1836 A.D.) constructed a very famous church at Sardhana near Meerut (Some sources mention the birth year of Begum Samru is 1753 A.D.). Walter Reinhardt Sombre, a European, was her husband who served many kingdoms. Sombre was granted Jagir of Sardhana as a gift for his service to the Mughal king Shah Alam II in defeating Zabita Khan (induced by NajafKhan). Begum Samru became ruler of Sardhana after the death of her husband.

Both Civilian and Military reforms took place during the period of Robert Clive. Under the civilian reform, a ban was imposed on the gift to officials and controlled private trade (Clive imposed conditioned ban on accepting gifts; i.e. for accepting gifts above Rs. 1000 of value, a pre-permission of governor is necessary). Under the Military reforms, he ended ‘double batta’ for European officers and from January 1, 1766 AD this allowance was only granted to soldiers who served outside the boundaries of Bengal and Bihar (except Allahabad).
Under administrative reforms, Warren Hastings in
A.D. ended the
dual government

system of Bengal by order of the Court of Directors. He transferred the State’s treasury from Murshidabad to Calcutta. Warren Hastings believed that the whole land belonged to the ruler. To reform in Revenue field, he chose
trial and error method
. Warren Hastings in 1774 A.D. was made Governor-General of Bengal by the
Regulating Act 1773.

The act provides for Governor-General and four consellors (“Council of four”), total five (including Governor-general). The Governor General was head of the government and had casting vote if equally divided. It was established to look after the affairs of Bengal. The Chairman of the Executive Council was called Governor-General. Several types of reforms in Police, Judiciary, Taxation, Faujdari related Acts etc. took place during the time of Cornwallis.
Asiatic Society of Bengal
was established on 15th January, 1784 A.D. in the tenure of Governor General Warren Hastings.
Warren Hastings and Wellesley were related to the
Ring-Fence theory

Impeachment proceedings were initiated on Hastings for injustices and atrocities committed by him but in the light of his service, proceedings which took place between the years 1788 A.D. and 1795 A.D. (until he was acquitted in April 1795) The following were the policies of Britishers towards Indian States (Princely States):-
1- Company’s struggle for equality with Indian provinces (1740-1765 AD)
2- Policy of Ring Fence (1765-1813 AD)
3- Policy of Subordinate Isolation (1813-1857 AD)
4- Policy of Subordinate Union (1858-1935 AD)
5- Policy of Equal Federation (1935-1947 AD)
Britishers developed a new system forjustice delivery through hierarchical institutions consisting of
Diwani
and
Faujdari Courts
. This system was started by Warren Hastings but Cornwallis made it more rigid. He concentrated all powers in the hands of
Collector
. In 1787 A.D. the District Collector was made the Diwani Judge of Diwani Courts and was granted some Faujdari Powers to deliver Justice in some Faujdari cases too.

In 1790-92 AD, District Faujdari Courts with Indian Judges were abolished and in their place four Circuit Courts, three for Bengal and one for Bihar, were appointed. These Courts were headed by European officials and the Justice was delivered with the help of Indian
Kazis
and
Muftis
. Cornwallis initiated his rule of
specification of law,
it was a set of regulations that codified administrative, revenue and judicial reforms of East India Company in Bengal.
‘Cornwallis Code’
is the collection of judicial reforms by Cornwallis in 1793 A.D. This reform was based on the law of
‘Separation of Powers’
. He separated Revenue and Judicial administration. The judicial and faujdari power of collector was taken back and he was entrusted with powers related to taxation only.

A new hierarchy of officers was created for jobs in the District Diwani Courts. District Judges were given works of Faujdari and Police too. The modern Indian Civil Services was reorganised and professionalised by Cornwallis (1793). He forbade private trade and gifts, raised salaries, separated functions and gave legal form to civil service rules; he was regarded as the reformer of civil service. Lord Cornwallis was the Governor General of Bengal from 1786 to 1793 and from 30th July, 1805 A.D. to 5th October, 1805 A.D. He died at Ghazipur (Uttar Pradesh) on 5th October 1805 A.D. His grave is present in Ghazipur.
Treaty of Bassein

(December, 1802) was made between Peshwa Bajirao II and Britishers. Subsidiary Alliance of Lord Wellesley was accepted by the Peshwa Bajirao II becoming the first Maratha chief to do so. According to subsidiary alliance, Peshwa accepted the offer of protection of English. As per the treaty, Britishers provided 6 thousands soldiers to reinstate Peshwa at Poona and the Peshwa promised lands are having revenues worth 26 lakhs annually as a payback.
Lord Wellesley (1798-1805 A.D.)

cleverly used subsidiary alliance as a tool to make Indian provinces as puppets of Britishers. He did not discover this method. This method was in practice earlier also but it gradually evolved and the final shape was provided by Wellesley. Dupleix was the first European to give his Army to an Indian ruler on the promise of a fixed payment to the Company. Britishers used these tactics too. First such instances can be traced as 1765 treaty in Oudh/ Awadh (can be marked as the precursor of subsidiary alliance) where Company promised to protect the boundaries of Oudh on a fixed payment to the Company.
The evolved version of the
Subsidiary Alliance
of Lord Wellesley was accepted by the Princely States in the following Sequence-
Hyderabad (1798 A.D. and 1800 A.D.)
Mysore
Tanjore (October 1799 A.D.)
Awadh
(November 1801 A.D.),
Peshwa
(December 1802 A.D.),
Bhonsle of
Nagpur/ Berar (December 1803 A.D.).
Sindhiya Bharatpur (1803-05)
(February 1804 A.D.), Some other alliances include Jodhpur (1818), Udaipur/ Mewar (1818), Bundi (Feb., 1818), Bikaner (March, 1818) and Jaipur (April, 1818).

Lord William Bentinck in July 1828 A.D. assumed the office of Governor-General of Bengal. He took some bold steps to eliminate evil social practices such as Sati system, Female Infanticide etc. On the will of Court of Directors, he tried to adopt neutral policies towards the Princely Indian States wherever possible. Mismanagement in Jaipur one time grew so high that the British Resident was attacked there but William Bentinck did not interfere. Similarly, he did not interfere in the internal matters of Jodhpur, Bundi, Kota and Bhopal when he had enough reasons to do so. Deviating from this policy, he placed Mysore (in 1831 A.D.) and provinces of Kurg (1834 A.D.) and Kachhar (in 1832 A.D.) under British Empire because of extreme mismanagement prevailing there.
During the seven- year rule of William Bentinck (1828-35 A.D.) the old policies of war and annexation were abandoned or reduced. William Bentinck is remembered for his contributions in the field of
Administrative and Social Reforms
By the
Charter Act of 1833
an attempt was made towards totally centralised Administration. Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India through this Act.
Captain Sleeman

was appointed by the William Bentinck to tackle the Thug Activities. He arrested 1562 thugs between 1826 to 1835 A.D. Many of them hanged and the rest of them were exiled. By 1839 A.D., the organiZed nature of Thugi ended.

By the declaration of 1789 A.D. the export of slaves from Bengal was stopped. Acts related to slaves were formulated in 1811 A.D. and 1823 A.D. The Charter Act of 1833 A.D. emphasized on formulating law by the Governor to end
slavery
as soon as possible. By
slavery was declared illegal in most part of British India (it removed the enforceability of slave property in civil courts). In 1860 A.D.,
Indian Penal Code
declared slavery as a crime. (IPC was repealed and Bhartiya Nyay Samhita came into force in 2024).
Anglo-Nepal War (1814-16 A.D.)
took place during the time of Governor-General
Lord Hastings (1813-23 A.D.)
which ended with
Sugauli’s Treaty
James Outram

was made British resident of Oudh replacing Sleeman. He said the administration of Oudh is very polluted and the condition of the people was miserable. This report of Outram emerged as the base for the annexation of Awadh. Lord Dalhousie (1848-56 A.D.) blamed Nawab of Awadh
Wajid Ali Shah
for
maladministration
and, in February 1856 A.D., Awadh was annexed by Britishers. The States that were annexed through the policy of
Doctrine of Lapse
are - Satara (1848), Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), Baghat (1850), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854) etc.

Lord Dalhousie formulated the first comprehensive Railway Policy for India in 1853 and strongly promoted railway expansion, though the earliest railway proposals predated his tenure (like early plan of 1832 and Lord Hardinge 1844 plan etc.). The first railway line was laid between
Bombay
to
Thane
in
. The Great Indian Peninsula Railway started the train travel in India.

Main Reason for the development of railways was to export raw materials from the inner parts of the country to different Ports of India and also open Indian markets to British manufactured goods. Its second objective was the swift movement of Army in remote and distant areas to easily suppress any kind of revolt taking place in any part of the country.
Railway expansion in India accelerated particulary between 1880 and 1900, while Lord Curzon’s contribution was mainly administrative such as the establishment of the ‘Railway Board’ in 1905.
During Dalhousie a separate
Public Work Department
was established and a significant amount was spent on public work through this body.
With the efforts of
Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar
, Lord Canning in 1856 A.D., passed
Hindu Widow Remarriage Act
. According to Act XV (15) of 1856, widow remarriage and the Child born to that marriage was legalized.
Dhondo Keshav Karve
and
Vishnu Shashtri

were two propagators of widow remarriage. Dhondo Keshav in 1896 A.D. established a widow Ashram in Poona. On August 2, 1858 the British Parliament passed the Government of India Act 1858, transferring British power over India from East India Company. The act legally abolished the company and created the secretary of State. This act led to Queen’s Proclamation.
Queen’s Proclamation of 1858

was the most important result of the 1857 revolt. This proclamation was announced on 1st November, 1858 AD by Lord Canning at a Court held in Allahabad. The 1858 Act ended the Company rule and put the affairs of India under the direct control of the British Crown.
Lord Canning
was made first
Viceroy
of India. Queen Victoria was made the ruler of India in 1858 AD. A Grand
Delhi Darbar

organized in January 1877 AD. This Grand Durbar was organised by Lord Lytton, following the ‘Royal Titles Act 1876. During this, Queen Victoria was proclaimed ‘Empress/Sovereign of India’ & conferred with the title Kaiser-e-Hind (Qaiser-i-Hind).
Under Governor-General Auckland, first
Anglo-Afghan
war took place in
Lord Lytton was the Governor-General when
second Anglo-Afghan
war broke in
. By Act-V of
1843 Slavery was abolished
(removed legal enforce ability) by Governor-General of India
Lord Ellenborough
. During his tenure (1842-44 AD) in March 1843 AD Sindh was fully merged into British Empire. The policy of
Masterly Inactivity
in Anglo-Afghan relations was started during Lord Ellenborough and continued till Lord North Brooke. This period is called the
Period of Masterly Inactivity
. This policy is often recognized with
John Lawrence

because during his time at the office, he got full chance to follow this policy and evolution of this policy took place in his time only. Masterly Inactivity word is taken from an Article published by J.W.S. Wiley.
First Census
took place in
during
Lord Mayo (1869-72 A.D.)
. Proper census took place in 1881 A.D. during Lord Rippon.
Lord Mayo
killed
during an excursion in Andaman and Nicobar Islands group by a prisoner named Sher Ali Afridi. Mayo was the Viceroy who was killed while holding the office.
In 1876 A.D., Lytton became Viceroy and changed his policies towards Afghanistan.
Vernacular Press Act of

1878 A.D. was passed during Lord Lytton. This Act is also called the Gagging Act. (some historians also called this as silencing act due to its strict censorship). Sir Erskine Perry termed this act as a dangerous step towards India’s right to expression. Sri S.N. Banerjee termed this act as lightning from the sky.
Sir C.P. Ilbert
who was the law member of Viceroy executive council, on 2nd February, 1883 in Legislative council presented a bill known as
Ilbert Bill

. This Bill was aimed at equalizing both European and Indian Judges so that Indian judges can hereby try a cases involving British subjects in various criminal cases changing the decade-old provision of barring Indian civil servants from doing so. This Bill was aimed at ending any judicial disqualification based on races. The Bill faced a severe opposition by Britishers as they perceived this as an attack on their privileges.
Lord Ripon
is believed to be
most pro Indian Viceroy of British India
. He made some lenient laws in favour of children employed in factories numbering 100 or more, this was called as
First Factory Act, 1881
. According to this act, a ban was imposed on the employment of children below
7 years
in factories and the working hours of children aged
7 to 12 years
were reduced to
9 hours
daily and they got
4 holidays
in a month.
Second Factory Act, 1891
made week holidays possible. Lord Ripon is known as the father of the local government.
Charles Metcalfe
removed the restrictions on the press, he is also known as the
liberator of Indian Press
. In 1784 A.D., Sir William Jones founded Asiatic Society in Calcutta and steps were taken towards
Archaeological Survey of India
Alexander Cunningham
was appointed as the Archaeological Surveyor in 1861. In 1871, Archaeological Survey was made a separate body and Cunningham was made its Director General.
During the tenure of Lord Curzon (1899-1905 A.D.) in 1901 The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) became centralized and the post of DG was restored and in 1902,
John Marshall
(who was appointed in 1901) assumed office of the Director General (DG) of this body. The
Ancient Monument Preservation Act, 1904
allocated about 50,000 Pound for the protection and maintenance of the historical monuments of India.
Gopal Krishna Gokhale
compared the rule of Curzon with Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb.
In November, 1905 Lord Minto replaced Lord Curzon and John Morley was made Secretary of State for India. They both proposed
Morley-Minto Reforms

(1909 A.D.) which granted separate electorate to Muslims. During the tenure of Lord Hardinge-II (Charles Hardinge) Capital of India was shifted to Delhi from Calcutta. He invited Queen Mary and George V in a Grand Darbar organized at Delhi which is known as
third Delhi Darbar (1911 A.D.)
. In this Darbar, the partition of Bengal was abolished and the announcement was made for the transfer of Capital from Calcutta to Delhi.

chapters.title: Economic Impact of British Rule on India

runs: The Indian administration was in British hands and was conducted in a manner subserving the interests of England.
Home charges

refer to the expenditure incurred in England by the Secretary of State for India on behalfofIndia. It includes dividends to the shareholders of the East India Company, interest on public debt raised abroad, Civil and Military charges, store purchases in England etc.
Interest and profit on private foreign capital were another important leakage from the National Income System.
For banking, insurance and shipping services India had to make huge payments.

In British India, a term Imperial Preference was often used for the empire-wide preferential tariffarrangement (Concession given to British Imports in India). Under these arrangements, Britain pledged to maintain free entry for most colonial goods while imposing tariffs on foreign imports. This resulted in, almost no charge levied on British Imports but Indian Exports were charged heavily in Britain.
Strong preference to invest in land property by the rich class of India during British Rule proved detrimental for the development of Industries as they were low on Capital Investments.
In 1793 A.D. Cornwallis started
Permanent Settlement
of Land Revenue. Permanent Settlement was called by different names such as
Istimrari
Malgujari
and
Bishwedari

. This system was launched in Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, Varanasi of U.P. etc. Around 19% of British India was under Permanent Settlement. A new section of Zamindars was announced as landowners who were to provide
of the total revenue to Company and were paid the rest
of the total revenue for their duties. In the Permanent Settlement, Zamindars were small capitalist.
Ryotwari System
was generated by
Thomas Munro
and
Alexander Read.
Alexander Read first implemented this land system in Baramahal district of Tamil Nadu. Later on, this system spread to Madras, some parts of Bombay, Assam and Coorg (a part of modern Karnataka) etc.
According to this system, the
Ryots
were given the ownership and rights to occupy the lands and they were required to pay the revenue directly to the government. By this system, the farmer was the owner of his land. A total of around
British India area was covered under this settlement. The rate of land taxes in this system was very high and the recovery of agricultural rent was handled very strictly.
Under
Mahalwari System
the unit for revenue settlement is the village or the mahal. The village land belongs to the village community. The community was jointly responsible for the payment of the land revenue.
This system prevailed in around 30% of British India covering United Provinces, Central Provinces and Punjab (with some changes).
The constant flow of wealth from India to England for which India did not receive any adequate economic, commercial or material return has been described by national leaders and economists as
‘drain’
of wealth from India. Before 1813 AD company had a recurring surplus which accrued from
profits from oppressive land revenue policy
profits from its trade resulting from monopolistic control over Indian markets and

exactions made by the company’s officials. The surplus was used by the Company as an “investment”, i.e. for making a purchase ofexportable items in India and elsewhere. Against the exports of goods made out of this investment, India did not receive anything in return. This system was brought to an end by the
charter act of 1813
From 1813 AD onwards economic drain took the form of
‘unrequited’
exports. Dadabhai Naoroji described the drain of wealth as the
“evil of all evils”
and the main cause of Indian poverty.

Dadabhai Naoroji was one of the earliest and most prominent propounder of the Drain of Wealth theory. He with his articles and books ‘England’s Duties to India’ (paper), ‘Poverty and Un-British Rule in India’, ‘The wants and means of India’ and ‘On the commerce of India’ propounded his Drain of wealth theory.
Romesh Chunder Dutt also emphasized the drain of wealth theory. In his Article
‘The Economic History of India’
He proposed that half of the net revenues of India is being outflowed every year.
Indian National Congress
in
accepted the Drain Theory in Calcutta session and announced that the real cause for frequent famines and the poverty of Indian nationals is the ongoing Drain of Wealth for the previous years.
Syed Ahmad Khan
was loyal towards British Rule and he believed that the development of Muslim Community could take place with British government only.
Dadabhai Naoroji
(1825-1917 A.D.) along with W.C. Bonnerjee established
London Indian Society
in 1865 A.D. which popularized the severe exploitation and the pain of Indian nationals.
Dadabhai Naoroji was the first Indian to be elected to the British House of Commons on the ticket of the
Liberal Party
in
In December 1856, the East India Company decided to replace the old iron made
Brown Bess (standardised musket)
with new and advanced
Enfield Rifle (musket)

. Dum Dum, Ambala and Sialkot were decided the place for the training and trials of the new Gun. The Rifle required the biting of the upper part of the cartridge by mouth the rumours was that catridges were deliberately greased. In January 1857, rumours spread that the cartridge contained fats of cow and pig. The soldiers believed this new Rifle is an attempt to destroy their religions by the British. It became the immediate reason for the Revolt of 1857. The first sepoys to refuse catridged related practice were at Berhampore in late February 1857. Later, the refusal spread to other places. On
29th March, 1857
soldiers of Barrakpore refused to use the fat-containing cartridges and,
Mangal Pandey

attacked and Shot and wounded two of their officers, they were sergeant Major James Thorton Hewson and Lieutenant and Adjutant Bebpde Henry Baugh, at Barrackpore. One of the reasons for the Revolt of 1857 was the
exploitative policies of Britishers
and it was the outflow of all the dissents and grievances of Indians all of a sudden as an explosion in Volcano.

Anglo-Indian historians believed the Soldier’s discontentment and the fat-containing cartridges were the main and important reason for the Revolt of 1857. But modern historians proved this as only a reason followed by several other reasons. The fat-containing cartridges were just a spark which started the explosions of the explosives which were accumulated due to
political, social, religious and economic discontent of Indians against the exploitative policies of British Rule
Revolt of1857 started on
10th May, 1857
from Meerut, where the
3rd Bengal Light Cavalry regiment

(85 out of90 cavalries) refused to receive the new cartridges and openly rebelled against the authorities. They fired on their officers released their imprisoned comrades from jail and marched towards Delhi.
Major General William Hewitt

had 2200 European soldiers but he didn’t try to stop this storm. Rebels captured Delhi on 12th May, 1857 AD. During the revolt of 1857, the message was conveyed by circulation of Chappatis (Bread) and lotus flowers, which is marked as the symbol of revolt.
Khan Bahadur Khan from Rohilkhand, led the Revolt from Bareilly. He was appointed as the Viceroy in Rohilkhand by Mughal King
Bahadur Shah II
Rani Lakshmi Bai

(Manikarnika) was born on C. 19th November 1828 at Kashi/Benaras (now Varanasi). At the age of 14 Laxmibai was married to Maharaja Gangadhar Rao who died in Gwalior. Rani Laxmi Bai was the widow of Maratha king Maharaja Gangadhar Rao. When Gangadhar Rao died by leaving his adopted son (Damodar Rao) as his heir, but the British did not recognise the adoption and imposed Doctrine of Lapse. Dalhousie by Doctrine of lapse, annexed Jhansi to British Empire in 1854.

In June, 1857, the revolt began in Jhansi under the leadership of Rani Laxmi Bai (the revolt in Jhansi was outbreaked/began by sepoys Laxmibai Later assumed control and led resistance). She died on 17/18 June, 1858 A.D. fighting
General Hugh Henry Rose
. On her death, Hugh Rose said,
“Among the Indian revolutionaries the women lying here is the only man.”
Revolt in Lucknow began under the leadership of
Begum Hazrat Mahal
on 30th May, 1857 A.D. She declared her minor son
Birjis Qadr
as Nawab and took to all affairs of the Lucknow into herself. On 21st March, 1858 A.D.,
Campbell
with the help of Gurkha Regiment regained Lucknow.

On 5 June 1857, the rebel repoys halted at Kalyanpur; on 6 June they returned to Kanpur, where Nana Saheb (Nana Dhondhu Pant) assumed their leadership. He was later proclaimed/declared Peshwa at Kanpur (on June 30, 1857 as recorded by R.C. Majumdar) and the war of Independence spread in Kanpur.
He was helped a lot by Commander-in-Chief (his General Military Advisor)
Tatya Tope,
The original name of Tatya Tope was
Ramchandra Pandurang Tope

. After being betrayed by a close friend Man Singh, he was captured when he was camping in a forest. Tope was captured on 7 April 1859, after a hurried trial the military court gave the verdict on 15th April 1859 punishing him with death by hanging and he was hanged on 18th April 1859 at Sipri/Shivpuri.
Kunwar Singh
led the revolt from Jagdishpur (currently Bhojpur district), Bihar. He was from Shahabad region of Bihar.
Maniram Dutt Deewan

in Assam declared Kandarpeswar Singha, the grandson of the last king as the king and planned an armed insurrection conspiracy. But soon after Maniram Deewan was caught and hanged for his promotional activities regarding the revolt.
Thakur Kushal Singh
of Auwa defeated the combined army of English and Jodhpur.
Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah

provided leadership to the revolt from Faizabad (Ayodhya) in 1857 A.D. He was a determined opponent of British rule. He was native to Chinapattan of Madras, but he migrated to Faizabad. He asked all the different religious believers to stand as one against these English foreigners and to wipe them out from India. About him, Britishers said a man of great abilities, of undaunted courage of stern determination; and best soldier among the rebels. A bounty of Rs. 50,000 was placed on his arrest (dead or alive).
Mirza Ghalib
saw the revolt of1857 A.D. with his own eyes. He was born on 27 December, 1797 AD in Agra and died in Delhi on 15 February, 1869.
Shindhiyas of Gwalior
helped the Britishers in the suppression of the Revolt.
Minister of Gwalior
Sir Dinkar Rao
was praised by European historians for his loyalty to English. Minister of Hyderabad
Salar Jung
was praised in the same way for his loyalty.

The revolt of 1857 was spread over a wide area and was substantially supported by the public. But still, this Revolt was unable to bring whole of India together. This revolt did not become an all-India revolt; South India remained largely quiet, while Bengal and Punjab were only marginally affected though parts of eastern and western India were involved.
Scindia
of
Gwalior
Holkar
of
Indore
Nizam

of Hyderabad, King of Jodhpur, Nawab of Bhopal, Sikh rulers of Patiala, Nabha and Jind and other Sikh Sardar of Punjab, Maharaja of Kashmir and other kings were actively helping the Britishers in suppressing the revolts. To these rulers, Governor-General Canning said, that
these rulers acted as barriers against the high and fast-moving wave of seas, in the absence of which we would have washed out from India completely

. The Educated Class didn’t show any interest in the Revolt of 1857 they generally remained neutral or sided with the British, viewing the rebellion as a regressive, reactionary and anti-modern movement; which was one of the major causes of the failure of this Revolt.
Lord Canning

(1856-62 A.D.) was the Governor-General during the revolt of1857. During the Revolt, he made Allahabad as an emergency headquarter. Lord Canning was the last Governor-General appointed by the Company and was the first Viceroy appointed by the British Crown.
Under the judicial reforms,
Indian High Court Act, 1861
established High Courts at
Bombay
Calcutta
and
Madras
. After enabling 1861 Act, the courts were formally established by the ‘Letters Patent of 1862 under Lord Canning. Under the social reforms Canning passed
Hindu Widow Remarriage Act, 1856
. The Sepoy Mutiny of 1857 is known as First War of Independence in India and as an Indian Mutiny in England.
Sir Syed Ahmed Khan wrote
Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind
which was written/ submitted in 1858 and published in 1859 A.D.
R.C Majumdar was appointed by Government of India to write on the Revolt of 1857, but due to differences with the government committee he rejected this proposal, and he published his book
“The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857”

on his own in 1957 (although his original proposal was turned down in first instance, later he became member of ‘Board of Editors’ for history of the freedom movement but later discontinued with this service & wrote independently).
R.C. Majumdar said,
“ It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that the so-called First National War of Independence of 1857 is neither First, nor National, nor a war of Independence”
Most important outcome of 1857 was the
Queen’s Proclamation of 1858
. It was declared on
1st November, 1858

in Allahabad by Lord Canning ending the Company Rule and putting the Realm of British India under the direct control of Crown. This declaration included no extension of British India’s then present territorial possessions no further interference in the religious matters of people, equal protection of law to be available to all. British stopped all further annexation of native states and kings were allowed to adopt.
Approximately after the Suppression of 1857 Revolt, ‘
Peel Commission

’ was constituted for the reorganization of Indian Army by British Government. The Commission divided the army on the basis of caste, religion, race, community, etc. The number of European soldiers was increased from 45,000 in 1857 A.D. to 65,000 by 1863 A.D. Indian troops were reduced from 2,38,000 to 1,40,000.The ratio of Europeans to Indian soldiers in Bengal was
whereas in Madras and Bombay it was
. After the Revolt the soldiers the recruitment of Gorkha, Sikh and Punjab is increased
John Bennet Hearsey
was the commanding officer of Barrakpore when Revolt of 1857 broke out there.
Viscount Palmerston
was the then Prime Minister of United Kingdom. His tenure as Prime Minister was from 1855 to 1858 and 1859 to 1865.

The Revolt was poorly organized with least coordination or nominal central leadership. The rebels lacked a clear understanding of Colonial Rule, they have a myopic views of forward-looking programme, a coherent ideology, a political perspective or societal alternatives. Although official sources record substantial Hindu-Muslim and inter-regional unity among many rebels, but many central leaderships lack unity and which proved to be detrimental to this revolt. Modern Nationalism was not known to them at that time, which led to everyone fighting for their own interests and not for the nation. Except with the common shared hatred for alien rule in their own land.
Brigadier General John Nicholson

died on 23rd September, 1857, Who was wounded nine days before while leading his men to capture Delhi. The Delhi was captured by British on September 20-21, 1857. Sir Henry Montgomery Lawrence Chief Commissioner of Oudh (‘Lawrence of Lucknow’), mortally wounded on July 2, died on July 4, 1857 in Lucknow in the 1857 revolt while protecting British residency. Brigadier General James George Smith Neill died in September 1857 while attempting to reach the Residency during the siege. Major-General Sir Henry Havelock was died on dysentery in November 1857 a few days after the siege was lifted. Sir
James Outram
and
W. Taylor
termed the Revolt of1857 as a result of a conspiracy of Hindu and Muslim. Outram said that
this was a Muslim conspiracy in which the Hindus concerns were used for the Revolt.
It was only a Sepoy Mutiny, according to
John Lawrence
and
Seeley
. According to
T.R. Holmes,
it was a war between Barbarism and Civilization.
V. D. Savarkar
in his book
“The Indian War of Independence 1857”
, termed this Revolt as an organized struggle for Independence. He said it was the First War of Independence.
Surendra Nath Sen
whose book
‘Eighteen Fifty-Seven’
was published in 1957 was commissioned by Indian government to write history of 1857 and was the first Director of the National Archives of India.
The revolt of 1857 causes other civil uprising because it gave confidence to fight against British. The immediate revolt was Indigo revolt.
The Indigo Revolt (1859-60
A.D.
took place in Bengal immediately after the revolt of1857.
Sanyasi Rebellion
occurred in 1763-1800 A.D.,
Santhal Rebellion
occurred in 1855-56 A.D., and
Pabna
uprising took place in 1873-76 A.D.
Indigo revolt
was started in Govindpur village of Nadia district in West Bengal. Farmers there stopped the Indigo cultivation under the leadership of two workers
Digambar Biswas
and
Bishnu Biswas

who had once worked for an Indigo cultivator. By 1860, Indigo movement had spread to Nadia, Pabna, Khulna, Dhaka, Malda, Dinajpur etc. The intelligentsia of Bengal through public meetings, journals and articles in newspaper popularized the movement.
Harishchandra Mukherjee
, the editor of
‘Hindu Patriot’
, played a major role in this. Through
‘Neel Darpan’
Dinabandhu Mitra
openly visualised the atrocities of Indigo plantation owners on the farmers there.
‘Vande Mataram’
song is derived from the famous Novel
Anandamath
written by
Bankim Chandra Chatterjee
. The plot of this novel is based on Sanyasi Revolt. ‘Vande Mataram’ was sung for the first time in Congress session of
Calcutta
Wahabi Movement
which continued from the 4th to 7th decade of the 19th century provided an organized and stiff resistance to Britishers.
Syed Ahmad Barelvi
of
Rae Bareli

was the proponent of this movement. He was inspired by Abdul Wahab of Arabia but, in India, the movement was majorly inspired by Shah Waliullah of Delhi. By the efforts of Syed Ahmad Barelvi, this ideology soon spread to Northwest frontier provinces, Bengal, Bihar, Kabul and Central provinces. He captured Peshawar for some time in 1830 but he was killed in the
battle of Balakot (1831)
. He introduced coins with his name in Peshawar. After the death of Syed Ahmad Barelvi, Patna became centre of this movement. During this period the leadership was provided by
Maullavi Qasim
Vilayat Ali
Inayat Ali
Ahmadullah
etc. After Patna, the branches of this movement were established in Hyderabad, Madras, Bengal, U.P. and Bombay.
The
Namdhar Movement
, popularly known as the
Kuka Movement

, was a socio-religious reform movement among Sikhs in Punjab in the mid 19th century. The movement was initiated by Bhagat Jawahar Mal (Sai Sahib) and Baba Balak Singh, who emphasised devotion to one God, spiritual purity and revival of Sikh religious values. It later developed into a powerful reform movement under Baba Ram Singh (1816- 1885), who organised the Namdhari sect and expanded its influence among Sikh masses. The movement was called “Kuka” because followers used to shout ecstatic cries called “Kuk” during religious devotion. Baba Ram Singh preached monotheism, prayer, meditation (Naam Simran) and strict moral discipline among followers. He opposed social evils such as caste system, female infanticide, early marriage, and the practice of exchanging daughters in marriage. He also popularised simple and inexpensive Anand marriages, promoting social reform and equality. The movement gradually acquired political overtones and resistance against British rule, which made British authorities suspicious of its growing popularity. The 1872 Kuka uprising in Punjab against cow slaughter and British authority was severely suppressed by the British administration. He died in 1885 while in exile as a state prisoner in Mergui, Burma (now Myanmar), where he had been held by the British since 1872.
Pagal Panth
was a semi-religious group founded by
Karim/ Karam Shah
. Tribal peasants organised themselves under Karim/Karam Shah’s son,
Tipu Shah
, to fight the oppression of Zamindars.
Tipu Shah (1852)
was the
leader of the Pagal Panthi movement
after the death of his father Karim Shah in 1813. Under him, the movement changed from a religious group into a
peasant rebellion
against
oppressive zamindars
and indirectly against the
English East India Company
. The main cause of the revolt was the heavy oppression and extra taxes imposed on raiyats (peasants). After the
division of the Sherpur zamindari in 1820
