Ramchandra Reddy, a landlord of that village donated 100 acres of land to 40 Harijan families to solve their problems of the land.
Bhoodan movement began on 18th April 1951, and in October 1951, Vinoba set the target of 50 million acres by 1957; though the movement continued beyond 1957 but later it began to wane.
Madras Labour Union

was formed in 1918 A.D. under the leadership of B.P. Wadia and V. Kalyanasundaram and it became the First modern labour Union. Buckingham and Carnatic Clothe Mills labourers were part of this union. Soon, two Labour Unions in Bombay, one at Calcutta (The Indian Seamen's Union) and four Labour Unions at Madras were established.

The Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association was established on February 25, 1920, by Anasuya Sarabhai (she became president of the association) and Mahatma Gandhi. It emerged following the 1918 Ahmedabad mill strike.
All India Trade Union Congress was founded by N.M. Joshi on 31st October
, 1920 A.D. at Bombay.
Lala Lajpat Rai
was the first President of All India Trade Union Congress and
Joseph Baptista
was the Vice President. Dewan Chaman Lal was its General Secretary (they all were among the founding members) The motive behind its formation was the establishment of
International Labour Organization
in 1919 A.D. So Indian labourers decided to organize themselves as labour unions. This organization was divided for the first time in
A.D. at
Nagpur
Jawaharlal Nehru
was president at that time.
Communist International
was founded in
March 1919
A.D. by
Vladimir Lenin
and
Bolshevik Party
of Russia.
M.N. Roy

visited Russia on the invitation of Lenin and joined communist International becoming the first Indian to do so. To stop the growing power and influence of Communist activities, some communist members were arrested on the grounds of a conspiracy held in Kanpur. This case is popularly known as
Kanpur Conspiracy

British government in 1924 A.D. started cases against M.N. Roy, Shripad Amrit Dange, Ghulam Hussain, Ramcharan Lal Sharma, Muzaffar Ahmed, Shaukat Usmani, Singaravelu Chettiar, Nalini Gupta, Shamuddin Hassan, M.R.S. Velayndhun, Dr. Manilal, Sampurnanand and Satyabhakta in Kanpur conspiracy. The government charged them with the conspiracy of establishing a revolutionary organisation in India.
Revolutionary period of trade union is believed to
A.D.. During this
M.N. Roy
Muzaffar Ahmed
Shripad A. Dange
Shauqat Usmani
etc. were the main leader of the Trade Union Movement.
In 1940 AD, M.N. Roy established
Radical Democratic Party
Saumendra nath Tagore
in 1934 established
Revolutionary Communist Party of India

chapters.title: Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (1919)

runs: Government constituted a committee under the Chairmanship of Justice Sidney Rowlatt, in 1917 A.D. with the objective to investigate and report on the nature and extent of the criminal conspiracies connected with revolutionary movements in India and recommending legislative/legal changes. Based on the recommendations made by this committee, an Act was passed in March 1919 A.D. which empowered to arrest/search/detain persons suspected of sedition/revolutionary activity (including without warrant/trial as per provisions). This Act was also called as an act of
No Dalil, No Vakil
No Appeal

. Rowlatt Act was passed during the tenure of Lord Chelmsford (1916-1921 A.D.) in 1919 A.D. In his struggle against Rowlatt act, Gandhiji used different stages of movements-Rowlatt Satyagraha-hartals/civil disobedience (1919), non-cooperation and Khilafat movement (began in January 1921).
First bold step of Gandhiji in All India politics was the
Rowlatt Satyagraha
On 13th, April 1919
A.D., a meeting was called to protest against the arrest of two popular leaders of Punjab,
Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew
and
Dr. Satyapal
. The meeting was organized in
Jallianwala Bagh Amritsar
on the day of Baisakhi.
Brigadier General Reginald Edward Harry Dyer

ordered to open fire on unarmed peaceful gathering killing nearly estimates 379 individuals and wounding hundreds more (cited by UK Parliament). After the Massacre at Jallianwala Bagh, Rabindranath Tagore renounced the title of Knighthood granted by the British Government.
Shankaran Nair
resigned from the Viceroy's Executive Council in protest against the massacre.
Hunter Commission
was constituted by the Government of India to inquire into the incident of Jallianwala Bagh Massacre.
C.H. Sitalwad
Pt. Jagat Narayan
and
Sultan Ahmad Khan

were Indian member in this commission. The commission in its report presented in 1920 didn't find government guilty in this incident. It was said that disorder sometimes becomes revolt. That is why Martial law was compulsory and it is fully justifiable to open fire at that huge gathering. Also, this commission said that incident was just as an error in judgement of Dyer.

General Dyer was directed to resign his appointment as Brigade commander in India after this incident but British newspaper presented him as the protector of British Empire and British Lords of assembly praised him as the
Lion of British Empire
. For his services to Britain, he was given the
Sword of Honour
. In March 1940 A.D., a Revolutionary from Punjab
Udham Singh
killed the Lieutenant governor (of Punjab at the time of Massacre)
Sir Michael O' Dwyer
in London to avenge the Jallianwala Bagh killings. Gandhiji was given the task of writing the draft of the report of Congress Investigation Committee on Jallianwala Bagh Massacre.
Montagu termed the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre as Preventive Killing.
Shaukat Ali
Muhammad Ali
Abul Kalam Azad
Hakim Ajmal Khan
Hasrat Mohani
and
Dr. Ansari
were members of the Khilafat Committee constituted to launch Khilafat Movement. Generally, the credit for the starting of Khilafat Movement is given to
Ali Brothers,
Shaukat Ali and Muhammad Ali.

Sultan of Turkey was considered as the Caliph/Khalifa of the Muslim Empire by the Indian Muslims. In the First World War, Turkey was fighting against the Allied countries. During the First World War, British politicians promised Indian Muslims not to disintegrate Turkey Empire, but as the war ended, the Turkey Empire was dismantled by treaty of severes and came to an end in 1922 (after Treaty of Lausanne, 1922), when The last Ottoman Sultan was deposed and left the capital of constantinople in a British warship.
Indian Muslims started hating the British Empire and they started a movement to protect Ottoman Empire of Turkey and protect the Caliphate.
Khilafat Movement which was started against the disintegration of Turkey Empire got popularity and pace when it was joined by Gandhiji.
Mahatma Gandhi
was elected the President of the All India Khilafat Committee, in the All India Khilafat conference held under chairmanship of Fazlul Haq held in Delhi on 23-24
November 1919
A.D.
on 24th November
Khilafat Movement accelerated with the congress session of December 1919 at Amritsar. Gandhiji looked this as a Golden opportunity for
Hindu-Muslim unity
. Thus Gandhiji supported Khilafat Movement to get the support of Indian Muslims in the struggle against the British.
During the Khilafat Movement
Hakim Ajmal Khan
renounced the title of
Haziq-ul-Mulk
given by British government in the year 1908.
Md. Ali Jinnah

(then a Nationalist) was against the linking of Khilafat Movement with the Nation’s freedom. He suggested Gandhiji not to bring religion in politics. He was against the Gandhiji’s participation in the Khilafat Movement.
Congress held a special session in
September 1920
A.D. at Calcutta and passed the resolution of Gandhiji on Non Cooperation. The resolution was opposed by several senior leaders like
C.R. Das and Madan Mohan Malviya
. In
December 1920
A.D. this resolution was widely supported and C.R. Das moved the resolution for Non-Cooperation in the Nagpur session.
Gandhiji launched Non-Cooperation movement on
1st August, 1920

A.D. A special session of the Congress was held under the leadership of Lala Lajpat Rai in Calcutta in September, 1920 AD to decide upon the momentous issue of Non Cooperation. Discussions were held on the Khilafat question, the Government’s failure to protect the innocent people of the Punjab and punish the British officers. The leaders decided that the only way to vindicate the national honour was to establish Swaraj through the policy of Non-Cooperation. The resolution of non-cooperation formally adopted in this session. The resolution of the Calcutta Congress was ratified at the regular session held in Nagpur in December, 1920 AD. The movement got widespread success in western India, Bengal and Northern India. During this movement, Motilal Nehru, Lala Lajpat Rai, Sardar Vallabh Bhai Patel, Jawahar Lal Nehru and Rajendra Prasad boycotted court and jumped into the movement. Gandhiji promised
Swaraj within one year

of the launching of Non-Cooperation Movement ifeffectively carried out, at All India Congress Committee. The plan was prepared for a total boycott of Schools, Colleges, Government titles, Government institutions, Foreign goods, etc. This Movement introduced the people with modern techniques of politics and made them hungry for freedom. Communal Unity and massive participation of Muslims was a significant achievements of this movement.
The movement destroyed the fear of British power from the hearts of people.
At the time when Gandhiji arrived in India, Britain was at World War I. He supported Britain in the war. Gandhiji was given the title of
‘Kaiser-e-Hind’
for his humanitarian work in South Africa, which he returned during the Non-Cooperation Movement.
Jamnalal Bajaj returned the title of
Rai Bahadur
Tilak supported the Non-Cooperation movement but his death on the first day of the movement
(1st August, 1920
A.D.

made him unable to see the fruits of the movement. Tilak agreed with the policy of non-cooperation with the British (as in June 1920), but Tilak opposed his method of boycott (especially boycott of legislative councils elutions established by the 1919 Montagu- Chelmsford Reforms).
Chauri Chaura incident
took place on
4th February, 1922

. At a place called Chauri Chaura in Gorakhpur district in United Provinces, police openly fired at a group of protestors participating in non-cooperation movement, after this, the angered mob burnt down the police station and killed all 23 policemen (3 civilians were also died). This incident is popularly known as the
Chauri Chaura incident
. After this incident, Gandhiji withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement seeing it becoming violent. On
11th
and
12th February, 1922

A.D. Congress Working Committee at the Bardoli meeting suspended Non-Cooperation Movement. After the events at Chauri Chaura near Gorakhpur, the Working Committee of the Congress resolves that mass civil disobedience contemplated at Bardoli and elsewhere be suspended and instruct the local Congress Committees forth-with to advise the cultivators to pay the revenue and other dues to the Government and whose payment might have been suspended in anticipation of mass civil disobedience, and instructs them to suspend every other preparatory activity of an offensive nature. The suspension of mass civil disobedience shall be continued till the atmosphere is so nonviolent as to ensure the non-repetition of popular atrocities such as at Gorakhpur or hooliganism such as at Bombay and Madras. On February 24th, 1922 All India Congress Committee organized a meeting in Delhi and a limitation was imposed on all activities that amount to a violation of law. In this session,
Dr. Moonje
introduced a vote of censure condemning Gandhiji’s decision to call off the movement.
Rabindranath Tagore

emphasized creative programmes rather than movements and protests by masses. He was against the burning of foreign clothes and wrote a letter to Gandhiji to adopt creative activities instead of mass movements. Rabindranath Tagore called the burning of clothes during the Non-Cooperation as unwise and he said he was unable to obey the same.
Kashi Vidyapith
of Varanasi in 1921 A.D.,
Gujarat Vidyapith
at Ahmedabad in 1920 AD and
Jamia Millia Islamia
at Aligarh in 1920 A.D. which was later shifted to Delhi, were established during the Non-cooperation Movement.
Madan Mohan Malviya
established
Banaras Hindu University
in 1916 A.D. and was its Vice-Chancellor till 1939 from 1919 A.D.
Central Legislature (Council of States and the Legislative Assembly) and Provincial Legislative Councils, which were established by the
Government of India Act, 1919

were boycotted by the Congress on the directions of Gandhiji and they didn't contest the elections of 1920. An atmosphere of hopelessness was created with the withdrawal of Non Cooperation Movement and the arrest of Gandhiji.
C.R. Das
and
Motilal Nehru

formulated a new ideology. They proposed that Congress should fight elections to enter the councils be a part of Government and should enter the Legislative Assemblies and the struggle should be continued by being within the Government. But this plan was rejected by the majority of congressmen.
C.R. Das
(then President of Congress) resigned from the President's post and organised a party within the Congress in January,
A.D. with Motilal Nehru and named it
Swaraj Party
. The mandate of this party was to become a part of Councils and hinder their working through agitation.
C.R. Das
became the President of the Party and
Motilal Nehru
became its General Secretary.
S. Srinivasa Iyengar
(founder of the Swaraj Party at Madras) and
N.C. Kelkar
were the other main leaders of Swaraj Party.
The Election of
Vithalbhai Patel
as the Speaker or President of Legislative Assembly in
A.D. is one of the major achievements of the Swaraj Party.
Chittaranjan Das was also known as
‘Desh Bandhu’
. The meaning of the term ‘Desh Bandhu’ was
‘Friend of the Country’
. Chittaranjan Das studied law in London and became an advocate in India.
One of his most important achievements was that he helped in the acquittal of Aurobindo Ghose from the
Alipore Bomb Conspiracy Case
. He said Swaraj should be for common people not only for some sections of the society.
Madan Mohan Malviya
was the founder member of
Hindu Mahasabha
The
Government of India Act, 1919
had a provision that a commission would be appointed after ten years to study the progress of the government scheme and suggest new steps.
An all White seven-membered Indian Statutory Commission popularly known as the
Simon Commission

was set up by the British Government under Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin in November, 1927 A.D. The Commission was to recommend to the British Government whether India was ready for further constitutional reforms.
This commission was chaired by
Sir John Simon
and had

Members. Since none of its members was Indian, it was opposed and boycotted by the Indian National Congress and a section of the Muslim League, headed by Muhammad Ali Jinnah and this commission was termed as
'White commission'
by Indians. The commission arrived in Bombay on
3rd February, 1928
A.D. Chairman of this commission Sir John Simon was a member of
Liberal Party
whereas
Clement Attlee
who was the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom during India’s Independence was also a member of this Commission from
Labour Party
Indian National Congress in its December 1927 A.D. session held at
Madras
decided to oppose Simon Commission.
On
3rd February 1928
A.D.
Simon Commission arrived in India and the countrywide strikes followed. The places approached by Commission witnessed complete strikes and slogan “
Simon ! Go Back
” was used as a protest in several rallies.
Lala Lajpat Rai
who was leading a rally in the protest against Simon Commission was severely injured in a Lathi charge by Police and he succumbed to his injuries.
Lala Lajpat Rai was a major political leader of Punjab who led the freedom struggle against the British Rule. He is also known as
‘Punjab Kesari’
Nehru Report (1928
A.D.
which had a provision for Dominion Status to India was prepared as an answer to the Simon Commission. It was prepared by an all-party committee headed by
Motilal Nehru
in which
Jawaharlal Nehru
was the secretary. This Committee had ten members including two Muslim Members. In this report, Dominion Status for India was demanded instead of complete freedom.
Constituencies at places reserved for minorities were suggested instead of separate electorates (joint/mixed electorates). This report also suggested the
fundamental rights
should be granted to Indians such as right of free expression of opinion; right to assemble peaceably and without arms; right to form associations or unions etc.
In 1928 A.D., Subhas Chandra Bose and Jawaharlal Nehru founded
Independence for India League
to demand
Complete Independence
instead of Dominion Status.

chapters.title: Lahore Session of Congress, Proposal of Complete Independence (1929)

runs: At
Ahmedabad Session (1921
A.D.
of Congress,
Maulana Hasrat Mohani
defined
Swaraj
as complete independence from all type of foreign control, demanding Congress to adopt
complete independence
as its goal.
C.R. Das was elected as the President of Congress's Ahmedabad session of 1921 A.D. but the session was presided over by Hakim Ajmal Khan (served as acting President) as C.R. Das was in jail.
At
Calcutta Session of Congress (1928 A.D.)
, Congress gave ultimatum to British Government either to accept the recommendations of Nehru Report or face a mass movement.
Inability of the government to take any action on the Nehru Report compelled the Congress to announce
‘Purna Swaraj’
as its goal in the historic
Lahore Session, 1929
A.D. headed by
Jawahar Lal Nehru
On 31st December, 1929 A.D. with the stroke of midnight Congress President Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru hoisted the
Indian flag of Independence
at the bank of
Ravi River
. Congress working committee at the sitting of
2nd January, 1930
decided to celebrate
26th January, 1930
A.D. as
‘Purna Swaraj Day (Complete Independence day)’
and to celebrate 26th January, every year as
‘Purna Swadhinta Divas’

. In this Session during his presidential address, Nehru said, ‘we have but one goal today that of independence'. Congress on 31st December, 1929 A.D. at Lahore Session announced resolutions which included:
(1) There is no benefit from Round Table Conference.
(2) Renunciation of plan of Dominion Status in Nehru Report.
(3) Word Swaraj means Complete Independence.
(4) All India Congress Committee (AICC) will start Civil Disobedience Movement when deemed necessary.
At Lahore Session, 1929 A.D. Congress Working Committee was empowered to start Civil Disobedience Movement. In February 1930 Congress Working Committee held its second meeting at Sabarmati Ashram and
Mahatma Gandhi
was given leadership of this Movement.
On
12th March, 1930
A.D. Gandhiji started his famous Dandi March. He, with his chosen companions, departed from Sabarmati to Dandi for the Satyagraha on 12th March.
After 24 days of a long journey (reached Dandi on April 5, 1930) Gandhi on 6th April, 1930
A.D.
at Dandi, broke Salt Law by picking up a lump of Salt at Dandi
. And with this symbolic act, Gandhiji officially started the Civil Disobedience Movement.
Subhas Chandra Bose
compared this March with the March of Napoleon from Elba to Paris.

An English Newspaper editor - Brailsford mockingly said. “Can an Emperor be unseated by boiling sea water in a Kettle?” On this comment, Statesman newspaper replied, “Mr. Gandhi can boil the seawater till they got the Dominion Status”.
Civil Disobedience Movement spread to the whole country in Gandhiji leadership. In Tamil Nadu, Gandhian leader
C. Rajagopalachari
started the salt march from Trichinopoly to Vedaranyam on the Vedaranyam beach of Nagapattinam district to break the salt law.
On
5th April, 1930
A.D., Gandhiji reached Dandi village and addressed the foreign reporters as well as Indian reporters and said
"I want world sympathy in this battle of Right against might",
On
5th May, 1930
A.D., Gandhiji was arrested before a planned raid of congress workers at
Dharsana salt works (godown)
and was sent to
Yerwada Jail
Abbas Tayabji
became a leader of the Movement after Gandhiji’s arrest and
Sarojini Naidu
became the leader of the Movement after Abbas Tayyabji's arrest. Sarojini Naidu led the raid at
Dharsana salt godown
. This incident was elaborated by American reporter
Webb Miller
In the North-West Frontier Province (NWFP),
Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan
founded an organization called
Khudai Khidmatgar.
They were also known as
Red Shirts

. This organization emphasized on the national unity also organized movements against British Colonial policies and demanded improvements in the condition of labours. Muslims of NWFR played an important role in Civil Disobedience Movement under the leadership of Khan Abdul Gaffar Khan. During this movement,
Garhwal Rifles
under the leadership of
Chandra Singh Garhwali
in Peshawar refused to fire at unarmed gathering.
Tribals of Manipur played an active role in the Civil Disobedience Movement under the leadership of
‘Gaidinliu’
a Naga tribal woman. The movement led by her is called as
Jiyatarang Movement (1930s)
After the Civil Disobedience Movement, Gandhiji focused on creative programmes. On 17th September, 1934 Mahatma Gandhi issued a public statement announcing his resignation from Congress. In
October 1934
A.D.
, Gandhiji
officially retired from active politics to devote all his time in the upliftment of Harijans. In
September 1932
A.D.,
Gandhiji
founded an All India Anti-Untouchability League and in 1933 A.D. he started a weekly newspaper named
Harijan
for the betterment of Harijans.

Viceroy Irwin released Gandhiji from jail on 26th January 1931 AD considering the increasing influence of the Civil Disobedience Movement. Talks between Gandhiji and Irwin started in February 1931 AD with the efforts of
Tej Bahadur Sapru
and
M.R. Jaykar. Gandhi-Irwin Pact
was signed on
5th March, 1931
. Sarojini Naidu termed Irwin and Gandhiji as
‘Two Mahatmas’
. According to this pact -
(1) Under the leadership of Gandhiji, Congress decided to
withdraw the Civil Disobedience Movement
(2) All political prisoners who had not convicted of violence were to be released,
(3) Right to peaceful protest at shops offoreign cloth and liquor shops,
(4) Permission to make salt in the Coastal States without Salt Tax,
(5) Congress agreed to participate in the
Second Round Table
Conference.
People were disappointed by this pact because it did not include the commulation of the death sentences of
Bhagat Singh
Sukhdev
and
Rajguru

. Biographer of Irwin, Alan Campbell Johnson termed the benefits to Gandhi in Gandhi-Irwin Pact as consolation prizes and said this pact was the only surrender of Irwin agreeing to enter into negotiations.
The Indian National Congress held Karachi Session on 29-31 March, 1931 A.D. with Vallabh Bhai Patel as President to ratify/ endorse the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (Delhi Pact).
In this session for the first time resolutions on
Fundamental Rights
and
National Economic Policies
were passed.
On some people opposing this session (black-flag demonstrations against Gandhiji) Gandhiji said, “They might kill me but they cannot kill Gandhism”.
This was the first session where
Poorna Swaraj
was defined.
Resolutions on Fundamental Rights and National Economic Policies were drafted by Jawaharlal Nehru with the help of
M.N. Roy
Subhas Chandra Bose termed this session as ‘pinnacle of Mahatma Gandhi's popularity and prestige’.
Simon Commission’s, two volume report was published on
10th June and 24th June, 1930

. Political associations rejected this report. Main leaders of Congress were in Jail. British Government organized the first Round Table Conference in London from November 1930 to January 1931 in an atmosphere of dissatisfaction and discouragement. 89 Indian delegates participated but Congress was absent from this conference.

Tej Bahadur Sapru, Srinivas Shastri, Md. Ali Jauhar, Md. Shafi, Aga Khan III, Fazlul Haq, Md. Ali Jinnah, Homi Mody, M.R. Jaykar, Dr. B.S. Moonje, B.R. Ambedkar and Sundar Singh Majithia, etc. were the ones who participated in the first Round Table Conference.
K.T. Paul
represented the Christians in this conference. The conference was inaugurated by His Majesty the King Emperor (George V) and was chaired by British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald.
Mahatma Gandhi
was the sole representative of Congress in the Second Round Table Conference held between 7th September 1931 and 1st December 1931. This conference was joined by leaders like
Sarojini Naidu
Madan Mohan Malviya
and
Annie Besant
. Gandhiji travelled to London on
S.S. Rajputana ship
and stayed at
Kingsley Hall

in London. The Second Round Table Conference ended on 1st December and Gandhiji returned without any gains. After returning, Gandhiji said, “It is true that I returned barehanded but I am content that the Flag I had been handed was never let down by me and I never compromised with the honour of that flag”.
The Second Round Table Conference was totally unsuccessful due to communal issues.
B.R. Ambedkar
was demanding a separate electorate for Dalits which was not acceptable to Gandhiji.
B.R. Ambedkar
was the only Indian to take part in all three Round Table Conferences.
The Third Round Table Conference was held between 17th November 1932 A.D. to 24th December, 1932 A.D. and Congress boycotted this too.

A consensus among several parties for the separate electorate for Dalits was not reached in Second Round Table Conference. The His Majesty Government's declared position (endorsed by Parliament) that ifcommunities failed to agree the government would devise and apply a scheme. As a result British P.M. Ramsay MacDonald find a solution (although Europeans, Anglo-Indians, Indian Christians got separate electorates in 1919).
On
16th August 1932
A.D. Ramsay MacDonald announced
Communal Award
. In this award, each minority group was given some reserved seats in Legislative Assemblies and elections to those seats were to be held by a
separate electorate
. Members of the depressed classes qualified to vote, will vote in a general constituency and they one also entitled to vote in a general constituency.

Earlier Muslims and Sikhs were considered minorities but with this award the Dalit section of Hindu constituencies also got separated from it and now considered as a minority. Now Muslims, Indian Christians, Sikhs, Anglo-Indians and others including depressed classes were given separate electorates which were available in elections at Provincial Legislatures only.
Gandhiji started his first fast unto death on
20th September, 1932
A.D. from
Yerwada jail
against the Communal Award which ended with the
Poona Pact
between
B.R. Ambedkar
and
Gandhiji
. Gandhiji didn’t sign this Pact. On 24th September, 1932 A.D. Poona Pact was signed between
Dr. Ambedkar
from Dalit section and
Madan Mohan Malaviya
from Hindu community.

M.R. Jayakar, Devdas Gandhi, P. Baloo, Gavai, Thakkar, Solanki, T.B. Sapru, G.D. Birla, Rajagopalachari, Dr. Rajendra Prasad, Rao Bahadur Srinivas, M.C. Rajah, C.V. Mehta, Bakhale and Kamat signed this Pact too.

71 seats were reserved for Depressed classes in Communal Award which was increased to 148 by Poona Pact (Madras-30, Sindh with Bombay - 15, Punjab - 8, Bihar and Orissa - 18, Central Provinces - 20, Assam - 7, Bengal -30 and United Provinces 20). (This number is however 147 in some books). Also, 18% of General seats were reserved for the Dalits in central legislature. After the
Poona Pact
, Gandhiji didn't show more interest in the Civil Disobedience Movement and shifted his focus towards the fight against
untouchability
. He founded
All India Anti-Untouchability League
which was later renamed
‘Harijan Sevak Sangh’
Ghanshyam Das Birla
was its first President.

All India Depressed Classes League was founded by Babu Jagjivan Ram. All India Scheduled Castes Federation was founded by B.R. Ambedkar in 1942 A.D., while All India Depressed Classes Association was founded in 1926 A.D. by M.C. Rajah. On
14th August, 1931
A.D., B.R. Ambedkar in a conversation with Gandhiji said that "History tells that Mahatmas, like fleeting phantoms, raise dust, but raise no level".

In May 1934, the All India Congress Committee met at Patna to set up a Congress Parliamentary Board to fight elections under the aegis of Congress itself. However, some of the members of All India Congress Committee held separate meetings and founded All India Congress Socialist Party, and this party was officially inaugurated in October 1934 A.D. The policies and working methods were to be decided in a meeting that was to be held in Bombay.
Jaya Prakash Narayan
was the convener of All India Congress Socialist Party in Patna, 1934. He was the general secretary of party and
Acharya Narendra Dev

was the President. The objective of the was to push the Indian National Congress towards a clear socialist agenda, focusing on full independence, abolition of landlordism and nationalisation of key industries. Its members were :- Ashok Mehta, Achyut Patwardhan, Minoo Masani, Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia, Purushottam Trikam Das, Yusuf Meherally, Ganga Sharan Sinha and Kamla Devi Chattopadhyay, etc.
Bihar Socialist Party
was founded by Ganga Sharan Sinha, Rambriksha Benipuri and Ramanand Mishra (in 1991). Sri Narsingh Narayan Azad was a socialist and was an important member of Bihar Socialist Party.
J.P. Narayan belonged to Bihar Socialist Party.
J.P. Narayan also known as
Loknayak
secretly organized Indian masses during Quit India movement with the help of
Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia
and
Aruna Asaf Ali
. On 5th June, 1974, he called for total revolution (Sampoorna Kranti) from Gandhi Maidan. He was awarded
Bharat Ratna

posthumously in 1999. In April, 1946 A.D., ‘Jaya Prakash Day’ was celebrated for the release of Jaya Prakash from prison. A rally was conducted in Bankipur Maidan of Patna where the release of Jaya Prakash Narayan was demanded and criticism of government policy regarding the arrest of political persons was made.
In May, 1936 A.D., 21 businessmen of Bombay signed Bombay Manifesto. The manifesto was against propagating the principles of socialism as conveyed by Nehru in Lucknow Session.

chapters.title: Provincial Election and Formation of Cabinet (1937)

runs: On the basis of Government of India Act, 1935, in February 1937, election results were announced of provincial legislatures in which Congress by defeating its opponents secured majority in five provinces.
1. Madras (159 seats out of total 215 seats) - Congress
2. Bihar (98 seats out of total 152 seats) - Congress
3. Central Provinces and Berar (70 out of 112) - Congress
4. United Provinces (134 seats out of 228) - Congress
5. Orissa (36 out of 60 seats) - Congress

Congress emerged as the single largest party in Bombay (86 seats out of 175), Assam and North-West Frontier Province. Only in Bengal, Punjab and Sindh did Congress not secure enough support from masses to form the government on its own. The cabinets formed by Congress after 1936-37 A.D. elections only lasted for 28 months. In
July 1937
A.D., Congress formed cabinets in
6 provinces
Madras
Bombay
Central Province
Orissa
Bihar
, and
United Province

and with the support of other parties Congress formed a coalition government in Assam (a coalition government was formed by Muhammad Saadulla in 1937, but later resigned and Congress government led by Gopinath Bordoloi took office in September 1938) and North-West Frontier Provinces. Based on 1937 results, Sir Sahibzada Abdul Qayyum Khan, formed a coalition government although Indian National Congress was the single largest party, the Congress formed the government there by moving no-confidence motion against Qayyum Khan. The inclusion of Indians into the Second World War without consultation led to the resignation of all Congress cabinets. On
22nd October, 1939

A.D. Congress cabinet of all provinces resigned as an act of protest. Congress coalition government in Assam under Gopinath Bordoloi was resigned from the government in November, 1939 and the NWFP government was also resigned in November, 1939. On the resignation of the Congress cabinets, Jinnah called Indian Muslims to celebrate
22nd December, 1939
A.D. as a
Day of Deliverance

Working Committee of Indian National Congress decided for abolition of feudal intermediaries/peasants proprietorship in 1937 A.D. as a result of which Congress governments in U.P. and Bihar passed tenancy bills. Congress secured 134 seats out of 228 seats in United Provinces and formed government on its own.
Govind Ballabh Pant
was the Prime Minister (Premier) while Kailash Nath Katju was Law and Justice Minister and Revenue/Home/ Jail Ministry was given to Rafi Ahmed Kidwai.
In Congress ruled states the reports related to Muslims grievances were in the following chronological order.
- Pirpur Report - 1938
- Sharif Report - March, 1939
- Fazlul Haq Report (Muslims Sufferings Under Congress Rule Report) - December, 1939
Subhas Chandra Bose
became the Congress President after being elected unopposed at Haripura (Gujarat) Session of Congress in the year 1938 AD.
In the year
A.D., Subhash Chandra Bose defeated Gandhiji’s candidate
Pattabhi Sitaramayya

and became president for a second time at the Tripuri (M.P.) Session of Congress. But he resigned due to his differences with Gandhiji on matters offormation of the working committee of Congress. After that, Dr. Rajendra Prasad became Congress President. After the Tripuri crisis in the year 1939 A.D. Subhash Chandra Bose founded
Forward Bloc
resigning as Congress President. This organization was based on leftist ideology (it was a left wing nationalist political party).

When the clouds of Second World War were hovering above Europe, Subhash wanted to take advantage of Britain and Germany wars (World War II) and sought freedom for India with a military blow to British Government in India. He believed in an old saying of Ireland
i.e.
“England's difficulty is Ireland's opportunity”
that is why he tried to persuade Congress and Gandhiji to take help of Britain's enemy to free India.
Butler Committe
kings selected
Sir Leslie Scott
as representative of Indian princes (he was retained as counsel by standing) before the committee to represent their point of view.
In December 1927A.D.,
All India States People’s Conference
was organized in which more than 1500 political workers from various states participated. Balwant Rai Mehta, Manilal Kothari and G.R. Abhayankar played an important role in its organization.
Jawahar Lal Nehru
was chosen the President of All India States People Conference in 1939 A.D.
Most of the Princely States were acceded to the Indian Dominion by 1947 (barring few) while territorial mergers/integration continued later. By 15th August, 1947 A.D., except
Junagarh
J&K
and
Hyderabad
all princely states joined the Indian Union and the remaining three too joined by the end of 1948 A.D.

British Government by the order set up - two independent Dominions; and suzerainty over Indian States lapsed (princely states had to decide their accession). which complicated the scenario of a merger of states to form one Union. This problem was handled wisely by Sardar Vallabh Bhai Patel and political integration of India was largely achieved (but territorial integration continued later).
On
26th October, 1947
A.D., Maharaja of Kashmir, Hari Singh signed the ‘instrument of accession’. On March 5, 1948 Sheikh Abdullah was appointed Prime Minister.
Standstill agreement was signed between Government of India (Lord Mountbatten Governor-General and Viceroy of India) and Nizam of Hyderabad, Mir Osman Ali Khan on 29th November, 1947 A.D.
World War II started in September 1939 A.D., Congress demanded the independence of India for India’s participation in the war. Then Viceroy
Lord Linlithgow
threw India into the war without the consultation from Indian people & leaders/ Indian representatives and declared an emergency in the country.
Congress working committee asked for the announcement of objectives of war and also demanded India’s Independence after war.

Congress passed a proposal and condemned the attack of Nazi on Poland also lashed the ideology of Nazism and Fascism. It stated that India could not be a part of any war that is fought for the protection of democracy because India itself is struggling to achieve independence from the British colonial rule.
Lord Linlithgow
on
September 3, 1939

A.D. announced that India will be standing against Germany in the war. Without the authorization of Indian Provincial Ministries, India’s inclusion in the War led to the resignation of all Congress provincial cabinets.
Second World War started with Germany attacking Poland on
1st September, 1939
and ended after six years in September 1945.
Neville Chamberlain (1937-40) and
Winston Churchill (1940-45)
were the British Prime Ministers during World War II (1939-1945 AD). Churchill's tenure was from the year 1940 to 1945 and 1951 to 1955.
The idea of a separate homeland for Muslims (an autonomous muslim majority territory) was first proposed by Iqbal in
Allahabad Session (1930)
of Muslim League in his presidential address. Whereas the word ‘PAKSTAN’ was first used by a student named
Chaudhary Rahmat Ali
in 1933 in his pamphlet
“Now or Never; Are we to Live or Perish for ever?”
(which later became Pakistan).
This name was derived from the five Northern Units of British India. These units were - Punjab, North-West Frontier Province (Afghan Province) Kashmir, Sindh and Balochistan. From
22 to 24 March 1940
A.D., the Muslim League held its session in Lahore which was chaired by
Md. Ali Jinnah

. In this session a separate Muslim Independent States was demanded (North-Western and Eastern Zones of India). In this session, Jinnah said that he would not accept anything less than a separate Muslim Country.

Sarojini Naidu termed Jinnah as an ambassador of Hindu-Muslim unity. Jawahar Lal Nehru in his book The Discovery of India, mentioned that Iqbal in a meeting said that "Jinnah is a politician, you are a patriot".
Two Nation theory
of Jinnah was accepted in the
Lahore Session
of Muslim League which was held in March 1940. This proposal was drafted by
Sikandar Hayat Khan
and was presented by
Fazlul Haq
on
23rd March 1940
. To commemorate this day 23rd March of 1941 was celebrated as (first) Pakistan Day.
After rejecting the August offer, the Indian National Congress started
Individual Satyagraha
under the leadership of Gandhiji. The Satyagraha was a symbolic moral protest against the policies of the British Government towards India.
Individual Satyagraha started on
17th October, 1940
A.D.
Vinoba Bhave
was the first Satyagrahi followed by
Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru

“ Sarvodaya is a term meaning 'Universal Uplift' or Progress of all'. the term was first coined by Mohandas Gandhi as the title of his 1908 translation of John Ruskins tract on political economy, "Unto This Last", and Gandhi came to use the term for the ideal of his own political philosophy.
Vinoba Bhave established “
Sarvodaya Samaj
” in 1948 to propagate the ideals of Gandhiji.

Considering the rising power of Japan, international community, especially United States of America, China and Australia pressured Britain for political solution settlement with India. Due to urgent need for British action to solve the political problem, Stafford Cripps arrived in India in March, 1942 A.D. to negotiate with Indian politicians.
After reaching India in March, 1942 A.D., Stafford Cripps presented a proposal whose major recommendations were:

i- After Second World War India should be given a Dominion Status which is consistent with the declaration (i.e. associated by common allegiance to the crown, while not subordinate in domestic/external affairs).
ii- Indians should be given the right to form their own Constitution for which the elected constitution making body will be initiated after the War.
iii- Any provinces not agreeing to the new Constitution would have the right to keep themselves out of the proposed Union. and to retain its present constitutional position.
Mahatma Gandhi termed this deal as a
post-dated cheque
on a falling bank.
Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru
and
Maulana Azad
were the official negotiators from the Congress side in talks with Cripps Mission.
During

A.D., a meeting of Congress Committee was held at Wardha. It was attended by prominent leaders of Congress like Jawahar Lal Nehru, Abul Kalam Azad, Vallabh Bhai Patel, Mahatma Gandhi, Aruna Asaf Ali, Achyut Patwardhan, Dr. Anugrah Narayan Sinha, Pattabhi Sitaramayya etc.
‘Quit India’
resolution was passed in this meeting on July 14, 1942. It was chaired by then Congress President Abul Kalam Azad.
On 7th -8th August, 1942 A.D., meeting of All India Congress Committee was held at Gowalia Tank (now August Kranti ground) in Bombay. Wardha Resolution was confirmed in this meeting.
After a few modifications, the resolution for Quit India movement was passed on
8th August, 1942
A.D.
Quit India Movement
for India’s Independence was launched on 9th August 1942. Gandhiji gave a statement before the official launch of Quit India Movement. The statement had the following important points.
1) Government officials should announce their support and devotion to Congress.
2) Soldiers should refuse to fire on their countrymen.
3) Students should quit studies only ifthey stood firmly on this decision until independence.

4) Kings should accept the sovereignty of their people and declare their province as a part of the Indian nation. Masses should accept the leadership of the king only if he sees his future in the future of Masses.
In his speech Gandhiji said :-
"I am not going to be satisfied with anything short than complete freedom"
. It may be possible that Salt Tax and drink evil, etc. may be abolished or stopped by the English Government but my words will demand 'Nothing less than complete Freedom'. Today I give you a mantra
“Do or Die”
. This mantra means that either we will free our country or will die fighting for Independence.
On
8th August, 1942
A.D.,
Jawahar Lal Nehru
presented the ‘Quit India resolution’ to All India Congress Committee. This proposal was supported by
Sardar Vallabh Bhai Patel
. The draft of this proposal was prepared by Mahatma Gandhi himself with the help of Jawahar Lal.
Hindu Mahasabha, Communist Party of India
Unionist Party (Punjab)
and
Muslim League
were not in favour of this movement. On
9th August, 1942
A.D., Quit India Movement was launched. In the early hours of the Movement, Gandhiji and other important leaders of Congress were arrested under Operation Zero Hour.
Gandhiji,
Sarojini Naidu
and other leaders were arrested and taken to
Aga Khan Palace

Members of Congress working Committee (Jawaharlal Nehru, Abul Kalam Azad, Govind Ballabh Pant, Dr. Prafful Chandra Ghosh, Dr. Pattabhi Sitaramayya, Dr. Syed Mahmud, Acharya Kriplani) were arrested and taken to
Ahmednagar Fort
Dr. Rajendra Prasad,
member of Congress Working Committee couldn't come to Bombay, he was arrested and kept at Patna (Bankipur) Jail.
Shivkumar
and
Ram-nandan Mishra (he was first arrested in Cuttack but later he was transferred to Hzaribagh).
were arrested in Hazaribagh.

Movement of 1942 showed maximum impact in Bombay, Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, United Province of Agra and Oudh and Madras but the participation of the whole country was necessary for this movement to succeed.
Lord Wavell
was the commander in chief of India during Quit India Movement (1942 A.D.). He served as Viceroy from the year 1943 A.D. to 1947 A.D.
Winston Churchill
was the Prime Minister of England during Quit India Movement.
Abul Kalam Azad
was the President of Congress when the resolution of Quit India Movement was passed. He was elected President in
Ramgarh Session
of Congress in

A.D. and after that for five years (1941-45 A.D.) no session of Congress was held and Abul Kalam Azad continued to be the President of Congress for these years. He was the President of Congress for the maximum years before independence, also the political scenario of India was very fragile during his tenure.

During Quit India Movement, a secret radio station of Congress was broadcasted from different parts of Bombay Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia played a significant role in the Quit India Movement. He directed the movement while remaining underground. He also established an undergraound radio station.
Usha Mehta
was an important member of the group of Congress that broadcasted radio being underground.
Louis Fischer,
an Americanjournalist, was with Gandhiji just before Quit India Movement as he came to India in May 1942 and spent one week with Gandhiji at Sevagram Ashram, Wardha. (He was biographer of Gandhiji).
Louis Fischer,
with American intellectuals
Pearl Buck, Edgar Snow, Fredrick L. Schuman
and
Norman Thomas
demanded India’s Independence.

Riots emerging out of Quit India Movement were widespread in Bihar and United Provinces It emerged as a revolt. Eastern United Provinces (including Azamgarh, Ballia, Gorakhpur) and Gaya, Champaran, Saran, Purnia, Shahabad, Muzaffarpur, and Bhagalpur areas of Bihar were self instilled centres of mass revolt.

August Movement of 1942 A.D. became widespread among the farmers. Some groups of farmers performed agricultural activities in the day and took part in rioting activities at night. Their fierceness and strength demonstrated the glimpses of the revolt of1857, that is why Viceroy Linlithgow in a telegram to British Prime Minister Winston Churchill termed this movement as by far the most serious rebellion after the Revolt of 1857.
During the Quit India Movement,
Jayaprakash Narayan
fled from Hazaribagh jail and became active in the underground activities.
Yogendra Shukla
too fled with J.P. Narayan on 9th November, 1942 A.D. but was later arrested in Muzaffarpur and sent to Patna.

On the speech given by Gandhiji during Quit India Movement (1942 A.D.), Pattabhi Sitaramayya said, “In reality that day Gandhiji was speaking after being motivated with the power of Avatar and Paigambar.
Rashtriya Swayam Sevak Sangh
didn’t participate in Quit India Movement. It didn’t participate in any movement between 1940 A.D. and 1947 A.D. till foreign rule ended.
Aruna Asaf Ali
was a famous freedom fighter. She will always be remembered for hoisting the tricolour Flag at Gowalia Tank ground (Bombay) during Quit India Movement.
ArunaAsafAli, Usha Mehta, J.P. Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia, etc being underground provided alternate leadership to the Quit India Movement when all other prominent leaders were arrested.
Establishment of Parallel Government at several places was an important feature of Quit India Movement. These were:-
Ballia
- August 1942 A.D. - Chittu Pandey led the Government.
Tamluk (Midnapore) Bengal
- From December 1942 to August 1944 AD the Tamralipta Jatiya Sarkar in Tamluk started the relief programmes for the persons affected by storms.
Satara (Maharashtra)
- A Parallel Government named
Prati Sarkar
was formed in August-1943 A.D. It was the longest-serving Parallel Government till May 1946 A.D. Its main leaders were - Y.B. Chavan and Nana Patil. There was a Parallel Government in
Talchar
, Orissa too for some time.
Gandhiji was released on
6th May, 1944

A.D. on account of bad health conditions. On Gandhiji's release, Winston Churchill remarked, “When we are winning around the globe how can we be defeated by this old man who is our enemy for a long time.”

chapters.title: Subhas Chandra Bose and Azad Hind Fauj

runs: Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose was born on
23rd January, 1897

A.D. at Cuttack, Orissa (Odisha) division of Bengal province. He graduated from Scottish Church College (Affiliated to University of Calcutta) in 1919 A.D. and passed the Indian Civil Services exam in 1920 A.D. He became president of Congress in the session of
A.D. and
A.D. In 1939 AD, he resigned from Congress presidentship and founded
Forward Bloc
. He went to Germany in the year 1941 A.D. He gained control of
Azad Hind Fauz
in the sessions of
A.D. He is often remembered as
Netaji
Gurudev Rabindra Nath Tagore
gave him the title of
Desh Nayak

Clement Attlee became British Prime Minister on 26th July, 1945 A.D. British Prime Minister Clement Attlee announced on February 19th, 1946 A.D., the dispatch of the Cabinet Mission for constitutional reforms. Cabinet Mission arrived in Delhi on 24th March 1946 A.D. The Cabinet Mission to India consisted Lord Pethick Lawrence was secretory of State for India Sir Stafford Cripps the President of the Board of Trade and A.V. Alexander, First Lord of the Admiralty. They arrived on March 24, 1946 A.D. and held extensive discussions in April with almost all major leaders of the country. The Cabinet Mission proposed a three-tier polity for India. The major recommendation of the Cabinet Mission was to divide the provinces into three sections i.e. A, B and C.
On 16th May, 1946 A.D. Cabinet Mission announced its recommendations and its main proposals were-

(1) There should be a Union of India, embracing both British India and the states, which should deal with the following subjects – foreign affairs, defence and communications; of India would be given Independence.
(2) The Muslim League’s demand for Pakistan was rejected.
(3) The Union should have an Executive and Legislature constituted from British India Province and Princely State Representatives.
(4) A Constituent Assembly would be formed with the representatives of Provincial Legislative Assembly Chief Commissioners Provinces and the Princely States.

Cabinet Mission also recommended reorganization of Viceroy’s Executive Council and formation of the interim government in which all the ministerial posts including war member would be held by Indians.

Gandhiji supported Cabinet Mission and said this proposal is the best document the British Government could have produced in the circumstances, while cautioning that their best may possible be harmful.

stem: The first cereal used by man was:

runs: There are mainly eight types of food grains consumed by modern human society, namely barley, wheat, maize, millet, sorghum, mustard, oat and rice. These plants were present in the form ofweeds in different areas, which were later grown as seeds by human beings at different places, in different times. stem: The earliest evidence of agriculture in Indian sub continent comes from –

runs: According to the latest research, the earliest evidence of agriculture in Indian sub-continent has been reported from the Lahuradeva site in Sant Kabir Nagar district, Uttar Pradesh. The evidence of human activity and beginning of rice cultivation at this site dates back to around 8000- 7000 B.C. Significantly before this research, the earlier evidence of wheat was found at Mehrgarh (located in Balochistan, Pakistan) belonging to around 7000 B.C. and the earliest evidence of rice is known to be near the bank of the river Belan, district Prayagraj, from where rice bran was found. With above reference, if Lahuradeva is one option, then it will be the correct answer, but if Lahuradeva is not an option, then Mehrgarh would be the right answer.

stem: Excavation at Navadatoli was conducted by –

runs: Navdatoli has revealed excellent evidence of both round and rectangular residential structures which are located near Khargone (Madhya Pradesh). The former measures about 1–4.5 m in diameter and the latter 5.6 m long. The roofs were probably made of hay, branches and leaves and were supported on massive wooden posts, 22cm in diameter, raised at regular intervals around the huts. The open spaces between the posts were provided with mud-plastered bamboo screens. The house floors were made up of silt clay and river gravel, with the surface coated with lime. The huts were provided with one or two-mouthed ‘chulhas’ as well as storage jars and other earthen vessels. This site was excavated by Mr. H.D. Sankalia, Professor of Deccan College, Pune. This site was the most extensive excavated Chalcolithic site of Indian sub-continent, which is determined to be between 1500 B.C. and 1300 B.C.

stem: In the Chalcolithic period people of Maharashtra buried their dead under the floor of their houses in the following orientation:

runs: The people of Jorwe culture lived in large rectangular houses with wattle and daub walls and thatched roofs. They believed in life after death and therefore buried the dead inside the houses under the floor. Children were buried in two urns that were joined mouth-to-mouth and set horizontally in the pit, while adults were placed in a supine position with their head towards the north (north to south). These sites were found in Daimabad, Inamgaon, Chandoli, Nevasa etc.

stem: Which of the following matches is not correct regarding the origin of Harappan civilization?

runs: About the origin of the Harappan civilization, many scholars have presented different views. E.J.H. Mackay has considered that the origin of the Harappan civilization was due to the migration of people from Sumer (Mesopotamia), while historians D.H. Gordon and Mortimer Wheeler considered that the Harappan civilization was the result of migration of the idea of civilization from Western Asia. In this context, Amalananda Ghosh considered that pre-Harappan culture matured into Harappan civilization. M.F. Rafique Mughal considered that the development of Harappan civilization occurred in the region of Ravi river at Harappa. He refutes the old belief that Harappan civilization was inspired by Mesopotamian civilization.

stem: Which colour was commonly used in the Harappan Pottery?

runs: The Harappan pottery is bright or dark red and uniformly sturdy and well baked. It consists of wheel-made wares, both plain and painted. The plain ware is usually of red clay with or without a fine red slip. The painted pottery was of red and black colours. Several methods were used by people for the decoration of pottery. Polychrome pottery was rare and mainly comprised small vases decorated with geometric patterns, mostly in red, black and green and less frequently in white and yellow. The colour- scheme adopted for painting was light black, chocolate or light red over buff or greenish buff background.

stem: Based on findings of excavation of Harappan Civilization, what are not true?

runs: (i) For all kinds of constructions, same size of bricks were used.
(ii) Mostly all the houses were single storey.
(iii)Main roads were on average ten meters in width.

In Indus Valley Civilisation both baked and raw bricks were used. Generally the dimensional ratio of burned bricks received from all the Indus towns was 4: 2: 1. However ornamental bricks from Kalibangan and curved bricks from Chanhudaro have been found. Hence statement (i) is wrong. Most of the houses built in the Indus Valley Civilisation were built with one storey only, but some houses were also built with two stories as evidence of stairs have been found from some houses. Hence statement (ii) is wrong. The width of roads in Harappan cities was generally 10 meters. Hence statement (iii) is right.

stem: A horned deity engraved on a terracotta cake has been recovered from

runs: From excavations at Kalibangan, a series of ‘fire altars’ on mud-brick platforms were discovered. A triangular terracotta cake found at Kalibangan had a carving of a horned deity on one side and an animal (goat) being dragged by a rope by a human on the other. This shows the way to the emergence of a sacrificial tradition in the entire era.

stem: Which of the following civilizations flourished on the bank of River Nile?

runs: Ancient Egyptian Civilization flourished along the banks of the River Nile for almost 3,000 years. Nile River is known as the ‘lifeline of Egypt.’ The Nile is a major north-flowing river in northeastern Africa, generally regarded as the longest river in the world. Indus Valley Civilization (India) and Mesopotamia (Iraq) are the contemporary civilizations.

stem: What is the correct North-South sequence of the following civilizations?

runs: The correct sequence of the following civilizations from North to South is: Aztec - Maya- Muisca - Inca.The expansion of Aztec civilization was on the Northern Part of Mesoamerica. Mesoamerica included the Region from central Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Northern Costa Rica. Mayan civilization was spread over the southern part of Mesoamerica. Moisca civilization was distributed in the eastern part of Columbia (South America continent), whereas Inca civilization is spread in the western part of southern America till the north of Quito and Santiago to the South.

stem: The oldest civilization in the world is

runs: The Mesopotamian civilization is considered the world's oldest civilization. This civilization developed in present-day Iraq and the surrounding areas. The Egyptian civilization (the civilization of the Nile) developed in the Nile River basin and is considered to have emerged after the Mesopotamian civilization.

stem: The first ancient civilization to develop the art of writing in a proper system was?

runs: People of the Sumerian Civilization were the first to develop the art of writing in a proper system. Their primary script was very simple and primitive. Cuneiform script of Sumeria is generally known as one of the earliest systems of writing.

stem: The term ‘Aryan’ denotes:

The word was used by the people of the Vedic period in India as an ethnic label for themselves as well as to refer noble class. Scholars point out that even in ancient times, the idea of being an 'Aryan' was religious, cultural and linguistic, not racial.

stem: Rights and Rituals related to Yajnas are mentioned in–

runs: Yajurveda in Sanskrit means ‘wisdom of sacrificial formulas.’ This Veda, compiled a century or two after the Rig-veda, contains prose and verse formulae that were to be pronounced by the priests performing the manual part of the sacrifice. It describes in prose about the procedural details of performing different rituals and Yajnas using the hymns of the Rigveda. The Samhitas of Yajurveda are divided into two parts: Shukla or white Yajurveda and Krishna or black Yajurveda.

stem: Which of the following Vedas is divided into two branches as Krishna and Shukla?

runs: Yajurveda has two major branches: the Krishna Yajurveda and the Shukla Yajurveda. In the Krishna Yajurveda, the mantras are irregular and mixed, whereas in the Shukla Yajurveda, the order and recitation of the mantras are more systematic. This Veda is related to the rituals and proce dures of sacrifices (yajna) and worship.

stem: The compilation of which among the following is based upon the Rig Veda?

runs: The Samaveda is the shortest among all the four Vedas. It is closely connected with the Rigveda. It has taken many verses from the Rigveda. The Samaveda is compiled inclusively for ritual application and all of its verses are meant to be chanted in ceremonies. Samaveda Samhita consists a total of 1875 verses. Among these except 75 or 99 verses, all of them are compiled in Rigveda.

stem: The earliest evidence of the use of iron in India has been discovered from:

runs: Atranjikhera is a prehistoric and historic excavated archaeological site on the bank of Kali river, a tributary of Ganga. This site was first identified by Sir Alexander Cunningham in his survey report in 1861-62 but excavated by R.C. Gaur. A Trial trench put in 1962, was followed in the next year by digging on a small scale. Regular excavation was started in 1964. The earliest evidence of iron used in the region dates back to around 1000 B.C.

stem: When did the use of iron begin in Indian subcontinent?

d: More than one of the above
e: None of the above

runs: The history of early iron smelting, practised by the tribal artisans in different regions of ancient India dates back to 1300 to 1200 B.C. Most of the archaeologists accept around 1000 B.C. as the start of the Iron Age in subcontinent. So earliest use of iron in Indian subcontinent can be placed around 3000 years ago. Hence option (e) none of the above is correct.

stem: King Asvapati of the Upanishadic period was the ruler of:

Some of them were- King Janak of Videha, King Pravahanjabali of Panchal, King Asvapati of Kekaya and King Ajatshatru of Kashi. Asvapati was a Kshatriya king. stem: Which of the following is the correct order of the Vedic literature?

runs: Each of the Vedas is divided into four parts (or sections). The correct order of them is Samhitas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads. Samhitas and Brahmanas form the Karma Kanda segment of the Vedas. Aranyakas and Upanishads form the Gyan-Kanda segment of the Vedas. They explicitly focus on philosophy and spirituality.

stem: The river mentioned most in early Vedic literature is:

stem: Which of the followings customs emerged during the post-Vedic period:

stem: While living in which Ashram did a person have to perform the rituals of the Pancha Mahayagya?

runs: While living in the Grihastha Ashram (householder stage), a person was required to perform the Pancha Mahayajnas (Five Great Sacrifices). These five sacrifices were: Brahma Yajna ,Deva Yajna ,Pitra Yajna, Bhuta Yajna ,Atithi Yajna. The Grihastha Ashram was considered the foundation of society, as it was during this stage that a person earned wealth and also supported the other three ashramas—Brahmacharya ,Vanaprastha and Sanyasa.

stem: The ‘Dharma’ and ‘Rita’ depict a central idea of ancient Vedic Civilization of India. In this context, consider the following statements:

runs: 1. ‘Dharma’ was a conception of obligations and the discharge of one’s duties to oneself and to others.
2. ‘Rita’ was the fundamental moral law governing the functioning of the universe and all it contained.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

Dharma and Rita in the Vedic period appear as early as the Rigveda. Usually, Dharma signifies cosmic ordinance often in connection with the sense of natural or divine law. ‘Rita’ as such is closely related to universal harmony in which all things in the world have a proper place and function. So the term ‘Rita’ means an impersonal law while Dharma characterizes those personal actions that engender or maintain the cosmic order.Thus, the correct answer is option (c).

stem: In context on Indian culture 'Rita' means

stem: The religion of early Vedic Aryans was primarily of

stem: In which of the Vedas, Sabha and Samiti are called as two daughters of Prajapati?

runs: The clear distinction between Sabha and Samiti cannot be made but it is clear that ‘Sabha’ and ‘Samiti’ were clearly mentioned in the Atharvaveda as the two daughters of Prajapati.

stem: In which Veda are Sabha and Samiti declared as separate institutions?

runs: Among the Vedic texts, Sabha and Samiti are clearly mentioned as separate institutions in the Atharvaveda, although both these institutions (Sabha and Samiti) are also mentioned in the Rigveda. In the tenth Mandal of the Rigveda too, Sabha and Samiti are mentioned and an appeal is made to create unity and consensus between the two. In the Rigveda, the roles of Sabha and Samiti are not clearly separated nor are they established in an institutional form, as we find in the Atharvaveda. In a verse of the Atharvaveda, Sabha and Samiti are shown as two separate institutions and they are called 'two daughters of Prajapati'. Therefore, by mentioning them as two separate institutions in the Atharvaveda, their social and political importance is underlined.

stem: The Rigvedic tribal assembly associated with judicial function was

stem: ‘Ayurveda’ that is ‘Science of Life’ appeared first in:

stem: Rig-vedic religion was–

runs: The most interesting aspect of Rig Vedic religion was its polytheistic character in which a number of Gods were worshipped. The Rigvedic Aryans worshipped nature with intense feelings and endowed it with an animated soul. Vedic Gods were mainly classified into three groups- (1) God of sky-Varuna, Mitra, Surya, Vishnu, etc. (2) God of space- Indra, Rudra, etc. (3) God of the earth- Agni, Brihaspati, Soma, etc. Whenever these Vedic saints worship any God, they consider him to be the Supreme God, this is known as Ekeshwarvaad. Other than this in Rigveda Ekeshwarvaad is supported by saying Ekam Satt Vipra bahudha badanti". Ekeshwarvaad of Rigveda included vision of Advaityavaad, Sarvadevtavaad and Bahudevatavaad. But the concept of one supreme God of Vedas is different from the modern Ishwarvaad.

runs: 1. There are no parables in Upanishads.
2. Upanishads were composed earlier than the Puranas.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

A parable is a short and simple story that teaches a religious or moral lesson. The Upanishads contain several parables and stories that are used to explain philosophical concepts and teachings. For example, the parable of the two birds mentioned in the Kathopanishad, and also in the Mundaka and Svetasvatara Upanishads, unfolds many nuances about the jivatma who is essentially a unique blend of the human and the divine. Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.

The Upanishads, which form the philosophical part of the Vedic literature, were composed mainly during the later Vedic period, while the Puranas were composed much later, starting around the early centuries of the common era. Hence, statement 2 is correct.

stem: With reference to the difference between the culture of Rigvedic Aryans and Indus Valley people, which of the following statements is/are correct?

runs: 1. Rigvedic Aryans used the coat of mail and helmet in warfare whereas the people of Indus Valley Civilization did not leave any evidence of using them.
2. Rigvedic Aryans knew gold, silver and copper whereas Indus Valley people knew only copper and iron.
3. Rigvedic Aryans had domesticated the horse whereas there is no evidence of Indus Valley people having been aware of this animal.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:

A coat ofmail and helmet made of gold and iron is mentioned in Rigveda. Possibly they were used in warfare. Indus Valley people were lacking in weapons and were possibly ruled by a class of merchants. Indus Valley civilization did not leave any evidence of using weapons. Therefore, statement 1 is correct. Rigvedic Aryans knew gold, silver and copper. Indus Valley people knew only copper and bronze. The use of iron spread in North India between 1000 BC - 600 BC. Therefore, statement 2 is wrong. Rigvedic Aryans owed their success in India to their use of horses and chariots and recently a site called Bhagwanpura has been excavated in Haryana (of Rigvedic period), where horse bones have also been found. Evidence of the horse comes from a superficial level of Mohenjo-daro and from a doubtful terracotta figurine from Lothal. Therefore, statement 3 is also wrong. So, the correct option is (a).

stem: In the early Rigvedic period, what was considered to be the most valuable property?

stem: Where did Mahatma Buddha’s ‘Mahaparinirvana’ take place?

runs: Mahatma Buddha delivered his first sermon at the site of Deer Park at Sarnath. Later he moved towards Koshala, Kapilavastu, Vaishali and Rajgriha to propagate the teachings of Buddhism. The king of Koshala Prasenjit with his entire family adopted discipleship of Buddha. During his campaign, he reached ‘Pava’, the capital of Mallas. At Pava, Buddha stayed in the mango grove of Chund, the blacksmith. There Chund provided him with large amount of Sukaramaddava, which resulted in sickness with the flow of blood and violent deadly pains, but Buddha reached Kushinara (Capital of Republic of Malla). Here he abandoned his body in 483 BC at the age of 80 years. It is also known as Mahaparinirvana.

Gautama Buddha, the founder of Buddhism, was born in 563 BC in Lumbini (now in Nepal) in Shakya Kshatriya clan of Kapilavastu. He believed in the theory of Karma. Buddha discarded Vedas and Vedic rituals. Instead, he believed in noble deeds and acts in place of Vedic rituals. He has given four noble truths often known as Arya Satya:
(1) Life means suffering.
(2) The origin of suffering is attachment.
(3) The cessation of suffering is attainable.
(4) There is a path to the cessation of suffering.
Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.

stem: The ‘Bodhi Vriksha’ in Bodh Gaya belongs to which generation of its family?

stem: Consider the following about the features of Buddhist philosophy -
